story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Glowed
story.subtitle: A true LEGO adventure, click by click

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Carpenter's Workshop (1932)
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping blue bricks into a tall tower. Juno sat next to him, walking his toy dinosaur across the rug. "ROAR!" Juno said, bumping the tower. It wobbled but did not fall.

Milo picked up one last brick to finish his tower. It was warm. It glowed soft yellow, like a tiny lamp. "Juno, look!" Milo said. The brick began to hum. HMMMMMM.

Juno leaned close. "It's singing!" he said.

The brick hummed louder. The bedroom carpet seemed to swirl like water. Milo held tight to the brick. WHOOOOSH! The boys spun through yellow light.

When the light stopped, they stood in a little wooden workshop. It smelled like fresh wood. A man in an apron was carving a toy horse.

"Well, hello!" the man said, smiling. "I am Ole Kirk Christiansen. Welcome to my workshop, in a town called Billund, Denmark."

"Where are we?" Milo asked, still holding the glowing brick.

"The year is 1932," said Ole Kirk. "I make wooden toys and ladders here, in my little shop."

Juno pointed at a shelf of wooden ducks and trucks. "You made ALL of those?"

"Every one," said Ole Kirk, laughing. "I just keep trying new ideas until one of them works."

Milo grinned. "I like trying new ideas too." The glowing brick pulsed, like it agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Two Little Words (1934)
chapters.text:
Two years zoomed by in a blink. Ole Kirk waved them over to a sign he was painting.

"I need a name for my toy company," he said. "Can you two help me think?"

Juno scrunched up his nose. "Something fun!"

"It should mean something good," Ole Kirk said. He wrote two Danish words on the sign: leg godt.

Milo sounded them out slowly. "Leg... godt..."

"In my language," Ole Kirk said, "that means 'play well.'"

Juno jumped up. "PLAY WELL! I like that!"

Ole Kirk squished the two words together. "L-E-G-O," he said. "LEGO! That's the name, in 1934."

Milo clapped. "It's perfect, because that's exactly what we're doing!"

"Some people later noticed something funny," Ole Kirk added, winking. "In an old language called Latin, the word lego means 'I put together.' Nobody knows if that's really why I picked it. But it's a nice little match, don't you think?"

Juno giggled. "LEGO means play well AND put together!"

The glowing brick in Milo's pocket buzzed happily, like it liked the name too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Big Plastic Machine (1947)
chapters.text:
Years flew by again. This time they landed in a noisy room. A huge machine chugged and hissed. CLUNK-HISS-CLUNK.

A worker wiped her hands. "Careful, you two — this machine is new!"

"What does it do?" Milo asked, eyes wide.

"It squishes melted plastic into toy shapes," she said. "In 1947, we became one of the very first toy makers in Denmark to use a machine like this."

Juno reached out and touched a little plastic duck sitting nearby. "It's smooth!" he said. "Not bumpy like wood."

"That's right," the worker said. "Plastic can be shaped into almost anything, and it doesn't splinter like wood can."

Milo picked up a plastic brick-shaped piece from a bin. "Could you make LEGO out of this?"

The worker smiled wide. "Funny you should ask that," she said. "We're already trying."

Milo turned to Juno. "We helped pick plastic for LEGO!"

"We did NOT," Juno said, but he was smiling too.

The brick in Milo's hand buzzed again, pulling them onward.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Wobbly Bricks (1949)
chapters.text:
They landed in a sunny toy room full of boxes. Inside were small studded bricks.

"These are new," said a man stacking them. "We call them Automatic Binding Bricks. We made them in 1949."

Milo stacked three bricks into a tower. Juno gave it a gentle poke.

CLATTER! The tower tumbled apart.

"Uh oh," Juno said.

"They do that," the man sighed. "They hold the studs on top, but nothing holds the bottom tight."

Milo picked up a fallen brick and turned it over. He peeked underneath. It was totally empty inside, like a little cave.

"What if something was inside here?" Milo asked. "Something to grab onto the bumps below?"

The man's eyebrows shot up. "That," he said slowly, "is a very good question."

Juno stacked the bricks again, just to watch them fall once more. CLATTER! "Again!" he laughed.

The glowing brick in Milo's hand hummed brighter than ever, like it knew something big was coming.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Tubes That Hold Tight (1958)
chapters.text:
A tall man knelt beside Milo, holding a pencil and a brick. "I heard you had an idea," he said. "I'm Godtfred, Ole Kirk's son."

"I said the bottom needed something to grab on," Milo said.

Godtfred flipped a brick over and drew little round tubes inside the hollow bottom. "Like this?"

Milo's eyes lit up. "YES! Like a hug for the bumps!"

Godtfred ran to a machine and made a brick with tiny tubes underneath. He pressed two bricks together. CLICK!

He pulled. It held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo shouted.

Juno pulled too, giggling as it stayed stuck. "It REALLY clicks!"

"This new brick got its patent — that means no one else may copy it — on January 28, 1958," Godtfred said proudly.

"Will it still click a hundred years from now?" Milo asked.

Godtfred smiled. "This brick is built so well, it will still click perfectly with bricks made long after we're gone."

Milo thought of his tower back home. "That's the exact same click my bricks make!"

"Exactly the same," Godtfred said, "because it's the exact same brick."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Whole Park of Bricks (1968)
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The light faded, and sunshine poured down. They stood at a gate with big letters: LEGOLAND.

"Welcome!" said a smiling guide. "This park opened right here in Billund, in 1968 — next door to the very first LEGO factory."

Juno gasped. Giant brick animals stood everywhere. A brick lion. A brick elephant. A brick dinosaur, almost as tall as a house.

"A DINO-SAUR!" Juno yelled, running in a happy circle around it.

Milo counted bricks on its tail. "How many bricks does it take to build something THIS big?"

"So many we lost count a long time ago," the guide laughed.

Milo imagined building a giant LEGO shark someday, as tall as the dinosaur. "I know what I'm building when I get home," he said.

Juno hugged his own tiny toy dinosaur close. "Mine's already this big... in my imagination."

Everyone laughed. The glowing brick pulsed again, ready for the next stop.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bricks for Little Hands (1969)
chapters.text:
Next they landed in a bright playroom full of chunky, colorful bricks.

Juno grabbed one. It fit his whole hand. "These are HUGE!"

"Those are called DUPLO bricks," said the guide. "Made in 1969, just right for little hands like yours."

"Do they still click with Milo's bricks?" Juno asked, holding one next to Milo's smaller brick.

"Try it," the guide said.

Juno pressed a tiny LEGO brick onto the bottom stud of his big DUPLO brick. CLICK!

"IT FITS!" Juno shouted, bouncing on his toes.

"Every DUPLO brick fits with every regular LEGO brick," the guide said. "Big or small, they all belong together."

Milo grinned. "So even Juno's big bricks and my little ones are part of the same family."

"Exactly," said the guide.

Juno built a tiny DUPLO dinosaur right there, stomping it across the table. "ROAR!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Little Yellow People (1978)
chapters.text:
The next room was full of tiny yellow figures, each one grinning.

"These are minifigures," the guide said. "They first appeared in 1978."

Milo picked one up. Its arms swung. Its head popped right off.

"Whoa, its head comes OFF?" Milo said.

"So you can swap it for a different head, or a different hat," the guide said.

Milo rummaged through a bin of tiny hats and faces. He found a little grey fin-shaped hat. "Can I make a SHARK minifigure?"

He clicked the fin onto a figure's head.

"There," Milo said proudly. "Half person, half shark."

Juno found a tiny dinosaur-tooth hat and clicked it onto his own minifigure. "Mine's a dino-person!"

The two minifigures stood side by side on the table, one finned, one toothy.

"Can we keep them?" Milo asked.

The guide smiled. "I think that can be arranged."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The glowing brick hummed one last time. WHOOOOSH!

Milo and Juno landed softly, right back on their own bedroom carpet. The blue tower stood exactly where they'd left it.

But something new sat beside it: two tiny minifigures, one with a shark fin, one with dinosaur teeth.

"We really brought them home!" Milo whispered.

Juno yawned a giant yawn and hugged his dino-minifigure close. "Play well," he mumbled sleepily, remembering Ole Kirk's two little words.

Milo set the glowing brick gently on top of his tower, right where it belonged. It gave one last soft pulse, then went quiet, waiting for next time.

Milo climbed into bed, holding his shark minifigure tight. "Goodnight, bricks," he whispered.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Ole Kirk Christiansen started his toy company in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**, making wooden toys and ladders.
He named it **LEGO**, from the Danish words **'leg godt,'** which mean **'play well.'**
In an old language called Latin, **'lego'** also means **'I put together'** — a fun match, even though nobody's sure that's really why the name was picked.
In **1947**, LEGO got one of the first **big plastic machines** in Denmark, to make toys out of plastic instead of wood.
In **1949**, LEGO made its first click-together bricks, called **Automatic Binding Bricks** — but their bottoms were hollow and didn't hold tight.
In **1958**, Godtfred added little **tubes** inside the bricks, so they would **CLICK** and hold tight.
Because the click-brick design barely changed, a brick from **1958** still clicks perfectly with bricks made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, right next to the very first LEGO factory.
**DUPLO** bricks, just the right size for little hands, came out in **1969** — and they click together with regular LEGO bricks too.
The first **minifigures**, with arms that swing and heads that pop off, appeared in **1978**.

story.title: Theo and the Pixel Who Rewired the Goalie
story.subtitle: One midnight glitch, nine levels of game history, and a save that finally works.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Green Screen at Brookhaven (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake at 11:14 p.m., definitely past bedtime. He was rebuilding the goalie in his Roblox soccer game, trying to get the keeper to dive the right way for once. His laptop screen flickered. Black, then a sickly green glow, like something out of an old movie.

A cursor blinked in the middle of the screen. Blink. Blink. Then it rippled upward and folded into a tiny glowing shape, a stick-figure sprite built out of square pixels.

"New player has entered the game," the sprite said. "Name's Byte. You built a goalie who can't save a single shot. Want to see where saving actually started?"

"You're a glitch," Theo said.

"I'm a tour guide," Byte said. "Put the controller down. We're going to **1958**."

The green light swallowed the room.

They landed in a lab packed with humming machines, at a place called **Brookhaven National Laboratory** in New York. A man in a lab coat leaned over a strange round screen that curved like a fishbowl.

"That's an **oscilloscope**," Byte said. "Scientists used it to draw wiggly lines of electricity on a glowing screen. Not exactly a PS5."

The man, **William Higinbotham**, flipped a switch. Two blocky lines appeared, a net between them, and a glowing dot bounced back and forth.

Theo's jaw dropped. "Is that... **tennis**?"

"**Tennis for Two**," Byte confirmed. "**1958**. Years before anybody even said the words video game."

A line of visitors waited for a turn. One kid swung too early and missed completely.

"Hang on," Theo said, watching the dot drop. "It falls faster near the net. Like real gravity."

Higinbotham glanced over, surprised a kid had caught that. He nodded, pleased.

"Built that in myself," he said. "A straight line felt boring."

Theo grinned. He'd just out-nerded a guy from the actual first video game.

"First point to Theo," Byte said. "Let's keep moving."

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spacewar! at MIT (1962)
chapters.text:
They landed in a cluttered room full of tape machines and a computer the size of a refrigerator, lights blinking across its front panel.

Papers covered every desk. Chalkboard equations nobody but a genius could read.

"**1962**," Byte said. "**MIT**, a university in Massachusetts. Say hi to **Steve Russell**."

A guy with messy hair flipped switches, racing against some invisible clock. Two tiny spaceships spun on a round screen, firing little dots at each other.

"That's **Spacewar!**," Byte said. "Built for a computer called the **PDP-1** — picture a computer that fills a whole wall, long before anything fit in your pocket."

Theo leaned closer, tracking the ships. "Wait. There's a star in the middle, pulling them in?"

"Gravity," one of the students said, not looking up. "Fly too close, you get yanked in and explode. Makes it harder. Harder's more fun."

Theo thought about his own Roblox obby, the one where players quit after one try.

"That's exactly what's wrong with my level," he muttered. "Too easy. No reason to come back twice."

He grabbed a spare control knob. "Can I try?"

Russell shrugged, already distracted by a stuck switch. "Controls are backwards for lefties. Good luck."

Theo spun his little ship straight into the gravity well and got vaporized in under four seconds. Byte made a wheezing, pixelated laugh.

"Recorded for history," Byte said. "Worst pilot of **1962**."

"I meant to do that," Theo said. "Pure gravity research."

Byte didn't buy it for a second. Honestly, neither did Theo.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box in a Spare Room (late 1960s)
chapters.text:
Byte blinked them into a cluttered home workshop, wires strung across a table, a plain wooden box wired to a television.

"**Ralph Baer**," Byte said, pointing at a man soldering a circuit board. "People later called him **the father of video games**. In the late **1960s**, he had a strange idea: what if a television could do more than just show channels? What if you could *play* on it?"

Theo watched Baer hook the box, nicknamed the **Brown Box**, up to the TV. Two white squares and a dot appeared.

"That's it?" Theo said. "Two squares?"

"That's everything, back then," Baer said, without looking up. "You try drawing a whole world with wires and a television."

Theo studied the squares bouncing the dot around, like paddles. "You need a scoreboard," he said. "People always want to know if they're winning."

Baer paused, soldering iron hovering mid-air.

"Write that down," he told an assistant. "Kid's right."

Byte leaned toward Theo. "This idea became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, released in **1972**. First video game machine anyone could actually plug into their own living room TV."

"Our whole console shelf," Theo said slowly, "started with a wooden box and some wire?"

"Everything starts small," Byte said. "Your soccer game started as one blocky field, remember?"

Theo did remember. He'd almost deleted the whole project twice.

An Odyssey screen flickered on nearby, a plastic sheet taped right onto the TV to make it look like a tennis court, since the game itself could only make white dots and lines.

"People taped **plastic sheets** onto their televisions," Byte said, "just to add color the machine couldn't."

Theo laughed. "That's the most old-school thing I've ever heard."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Quarters in the Arcade (1972)
chapters.text:
The air smelled like popcorn and buzzing neon. Byte had landed them inside a bar lined with a brand-new machine labeled **PONG**.

"Different guys, same year," Byte said. "**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari**, also in **1972**. Their arcade game: **Pong**. Two paddles, one ball, dead simple."

Theo watched a line of grown-ups waiting their turn, feeding coins into a slot.

"It's basically table tennis," Theo said. "Why's everyone obsessed?"

"Because nothing like it existed in a bar before," Byte said. "Simple doesn't mean boring. Ask any goalie."

Theo, goalie himself on weekends, couldn't argue with that.

The sound was one single blocky beep, nothing fancy, nothing like the swelling music in Theo's own Roblox levels. The crowd around the machine didn't care. They cheered like it was a World Cup final.

A worker in an apron banged on the side of the machine, muttering.

"Jammed again," the worker groaned, pulling out the coin box. "Stuffed completely full. Had to call Bushnell himself to come look."

Byte lowered his voice. "Story goes, one of the very first Pong machines got so stuffed with quarters it actually broke. Might be a little exaggerated by now, after being retold a hundred times. But it tells you how fast people fell for this thing."

Theo grinned, picturing coins spilling across the floor like a jackpot.

He stepped up for his turn, gripped the dial, and sent the ball zipping past the computer's paddle.

**BEEP-BOOP.** Point, Theo.

"Not bad for a kid who usually just builds the games," Byte said.

"I play plenty," Theo said. "Someone's gotta test my own levels."

chapters.heading: Level 5: One Plastic Cartridge, A Thousand Games (1977)
chapters.text:
Byte's next stop was a crowded toy store, shelves stacked high with boxes.

"**1977**," Byte said. "Atari releases the **Atari 2600**. Before this, most machines could only play the one game built inside them."

Theo picked up a slim plastic rectangle from a display, no bigger than a deck of cards.

"A **cartridge**," Byte said. "Slide one in, play one game. Pop it out, slide in another. Suddenly one machine could play hundreds of games, not just one."

"That's basically like..." Theo turned it over in his hands. "Downloading a new game, but you can hold it."

"Exactly like that," Byte said. "You're not as different from 1977 as you think."

The green glow shifted them into a packed, noisy arcade a year later. Rows of blocky aliens marched across a screen, dropping lower with every pass.

"**Space Invaders**," Byte said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called **Taito**. It set off a craze. Arcades everywhere couldn't keep machines in stock."

Theo watched the aliens speed up as there were fewer of them left on screen.

"Wait," Theo said. "They get faster the more you clear? That's not a bug, that's brilliant. Keeps you sweating till the very last one."

"Nishikado didn't even plan that," Byte said. "His computer just ran faster with less on screen to draw. He kept the happy accident."

Theo filed that away. His own obby had a glitch that accidentally made the last jump feel epic. Maybe he shouldn't fix it after all.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Pizza With a Slice Missing (1980)
chapters.text:
They landed in Japan, a design studio smelling faintly of takeout.

"**1980**," Byte said. "Namco designer **Toru Iwatani**, working on something totally different from shooting aliens."

A sketch pad on the desk showed a yellow circle with a wedge cut out.

"Some say he got the idea from a pizza missing a slice," Byte said. "Nobody's totally sure, but look what it became."

The sketch flickered into a glowing maze. A yellow circle chomped dots, chased by four colorful ghosts.

"**Pac-Man**," Theo breathed. "I know this one."

"Everybody knows this one," Byte said. "That's the point."

Theo watched Pac-Man grab a flashing fruit and suddenly turn the tables, chasing the ghosts instead.

"Power pellet," Theo said. "Smart. Changes who's hunting who."

"Noted by a ten-year-old game designer," Byte said. "Iwatani would be thrilled."

The green light flickered, years spinning past, landing them in a warehouse stacked to the ceiling with unsold game boxes.

"**1983**," Byte said, tone shifting to something more careful. "Too many rushed, low-quality games flooded store shelves. People stopped trusting video games. Sales crashed hard across North America."

Theo frowned at the stacked boxes. "That sounds like it should've been the end."

"Felt like it, for a while," Byte said. "Some unsold cartridges, including a game based on the movie **E.T.**, got buried out in a landfill in New Mexico — basically a giant dump for trash."

"They buried video games? Like treasure?"

"Sort of the opposite of treasure, at the time," Byte said. "But in **2014**, diggers actually went out there and found them. Proved the whole story true. Those cartridges are basically museum pieces now."

Theo laughed. "Trash becomes history. Love that for them."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and Some Falling Blocks (1984-1985)
chapters.text:
Byte flickered them first into a quiet computer center in Moscow.

"**1984**," Byte said. "Soviet scientist **Alexey Pajitnov** is about to accidentally invent one of the most addictive games ever made."

A screen glowed with colorful blocks of different shapes, falling slowly, stacking up.

"**Tetris**," Byte said. "Pajitnov made it just for fun, to test out a computer. Simple rule: fit the falling shapes together, clear the lines."

Theo watched a long thin piece drop into a narrow gap, clearing four rows at once.

"That's so satisfying," Theo said. "Why does that feel so good?"

"Ask literally anyone who's played it at 2 a.m.," Byte said. "You're not alone there, either."

The scene shifted. A toy store in America, **1985**, shelves nearly bare after the crash from two years back.

"Nintendo needed to fix this," Byte said. "They released the **NES**, bundled with a game that would save the whole industry."

A screen flickered on, showing a mustached man in overalls running right, jumping on a mushroom-shaped enemy.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," Byte said. "Designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto**. Starred a plumber named Mario. Still the most famous character in games."

Theo watched Mario bounce a block, popping out a coin.

"Why's he a plumber?" Theo asked.

"Honestly? Nobody really explains it," Byte said. "Doesn't matter. He jumps good."

Theo tried the controls, timed a jump, and landed square on a Goomba's head.

"Still works," Theo said, grinning. "Forty years later and the jump still feels good."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Decade Everything Sped Up (1991-2011)
chapters.text:
Byte didn't even bother landing fully this time. The green light just kept flickering through scenes like a fast-forward button stuck on.

"**1991**," Byte said. "Sega needed their own hero to compete with Mario. Say hi to **Sonic the Hedgehog**. Blue, fast, impatient, basically a soccer player who skipped leg day and got rocket boots instead."

A blue blur zipped past so fast Theo barely saw it.

"**1993**," Byte continued. "A game called **Doom** lets players battle each other on computers wired together in the same room, called a **LAN party**. Friends yelling across a living room instead of texting."

"That's basically a Roblox server with extra cables," Theo said.

"Pretty much," Byte said. "**1994**, Sony jumps into consoles with the **PlayStation**, using CDs instead of cartridges. Fuller sound, smoother video."

The scene blurred again.

"**2006**, Nintendo's **Wii** lets you swing a remote like an actual tennis racket or sword. Grandparents suddenly gaming."

Theo laughed, picturing it.

"And **2011**," Byte said, slowing at last, "a Swedish developer named **Markus Persson**, people called him **Notch**, releases a blocky little game called **Minecraft**."

Green cubes stacked into a mountain, a tiny pixel character chopping a tree.

Theo's whole face lit up. "I've played this literally every day of my life."

"It became the best-selling video game ever made," Byte said. "Not because it had the fanciest graphics. Because it let players build whatever they wanted."

Theo looked at his own hands, picturing the half-finished soccer stadium waiting back in Roblox Studio.

"That's what I'm doing too," he said slowly. "Building something people get to mess around in."

"Welcome to the club," Byte said. "You've been in it this whole time."

chapters.heading: Level 9: Back to the Goalie Who Couldn't Save
chapters.text:
One more flicker, green folding back into black, and Theo was staring at his own ceiling fan again.

His laptop sat right where he'd left it, cursor blinking in his half-finished Roblox soccer game.

"One last stop," Byte said, voice coming from the speaker now instead of the screen. "**2015**. A museum called **The Strong**, in Rochester, New York, opened the **World Video Game Hall of Fame** — basically a trophy case for games that changed everything. Pong's in there. So is Tetris. So is Mario."

"Will my game ever be in there?" Theo asked, only half joking.

"Depends," Byte said. "You gonna fix that goalie, or not?"

Theo looked at his screen. The keeper still dove the wrong way every single time, exactly like when this whole night started.

He thought about Higinbotham's dot, falling faster near the net because gravity mattered. He thought about Space Invaders speeding up by accident, and Iwatani's power pellet flipping who was chasing who. Little tweaks. Huge difference.

Theo typed one line of code, making the goalie actually watch where the ball was aimed instead of guessing randomly.

He hit play. The ball sailed left. The keeper dove left. Clean save.

"THAT'S IT!" Theo said, way too loud for midnight.

Down the hall, a door creaked, a parent checking on the noise. Theo clicked the laptop shut just in time, grinning in the dark.

On the screen, before it went black, one tiny green cursor blinked once, like a wink.

"Not bad," Byte's voice said, fading, "for the next name in the Hall of Fame."

Theo closed his eyes, already picturing tomorrow: new levels, new saves, a whole stadium left to build.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a whole stadium left to build.

true_facts.text: In **1958**, physicist **William Higinbotham** built **Tennis for Two**, a bouncing-dot tennis game shown on a curved screen called an **oscilloscope** at **Brookhaven National Laboratory**.
In **1962**, **MIT** student **Steve Russell** and his friends programmed **Spacewar!**, a spaceship dueling game, on a giant computer called the **PDP-1**.
Engineer **Ralph Baer**, later nicknamed **the father of video games**, built an early TV game called the **Brown Box** in the late **1960s**.
Baer's **Brown Box** became the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game machine anyone could plug into their own TV, released in **1972**.
Also in **1972**, **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari** and released the arcade hit **Pong**.
A popular story says an early **Pong** machine got so stuffed with quarters it jammed completely — probably stretched a bit in the retelling, but it shows how fast people fell for the game.
The **Atari 2600**, released in **1977**, let players swap in plastic **cartridges** to play lots of different games on one machine.
In **1978**, designer **Tomohiro Nishikado** created **Space Invaders**, setting off a huge arcade craze.
In **1980**, designer **Toru Iwatani** created **Pac-Man** — some say the shape came from a pizza missing a slice.
In **1983**, stores got flooded with rushed, low-quality games, and video game sales crashed hard across North America.
Nintendo brought the market back in **1985** with the **NES**, bundled together with **Super Mario Bros.**
**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed **Super Mario Bros.** in **1985**, starring a jumping plumber named Mario, now gaming's most famous character.
In **1984**, Soviet scientist **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** at a computer center in Moscow.
Developer **Markus 'Notch' Persson** released **Minecraft** in **2011**; it went on to become the best-selling video game ever made.

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick That Dove Deep
story.subtitle: A WHOOOOSH into the deep blue world of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Blue
chapters.text:
Milo sat on his bedroom floor, building a new LEGO tower. Juno sat next to him, roaring like a dinosaur at every wobbly brick.

It had been one whole week since their giant tower went CLICK and held tight. Tonight, Milo picked up the old red brick from the very top.

It felt warm. Then it turned blue. Then it glowed like the inside of a wave.

"Juno, look!" Milo said. "It's doing the thing again!"

The brick clicked twice, loud and bright. **WHOOOOSH!** The whole room swirled like water, and the walls turned into deep blue ocean.

Milo and Juno landed with a soft splash, inside a floaty bubble deep under the sea. A smooth, silvery shape swam close. It had no hard bones at all — just bendy stuff, like the squishy part of your ear.

"That bendy stuff is called **cartilage**," said a bubbly voice. A small shark popped its head into the bubble, grinning. "I'm Finn. I'm your guide tonight. Sharks like me have **cartilage** instead of hard bones."

Juno gasped. "Are you older than dinosaurs?"

"Sharks have swum in the sea for more than **400 million years**," Finn said. "That means SO, so long ago, way before dinosaurs even stomped around. Want to swim back and see?"

"YES!" shouted Juno.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
Finn led them through swirly blue water. Something enormous drifted by in the dark, bigger than a school bus.

Juno squealed. "Is it going to get us?"

"Don't worry," Finn said quickly. "That's just an old shadow. This giant shark isn't here anymore. It's called Megalodon, and it's **extinct** — that means it doesn't live anywhere now."

Milo spotted something shiny on the sea floor. He scooped it up. It was a tooth as long as his hand.

"Is this really a tooth?" Milo asked.

"It sure is," said Finn. "It's a **fossil** — a tooth turned hard as rock after millions of years. Megalodon's whole body was bendy, so only its teeth stuck around for us to find."

"Sharks have SO many teeth," Milo said, counting on his fingers.

"Thousands and thousands," Finn said. "New teeth keep moving forward, their whole life long, to replace the old ones."

Juno grinned a big toothy grin of her own. "I only have TWENTY!"

Milo laughed so hard he nearly dropped the fossil tooth. He tucked it carefully into his pocket instead.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Biggest, Gentlest Fish
chapters.text:
A huge shadow blocked out the sunlight above them. Milo looked up, eyes wide.

"That is SO big," he said. "Is it scary?"

"Guess what it eats," Finn said, smiling.

Milo thought hard. "Big teeth? Big bites?"

"Nope!" Finn said. "Meet the whale shark, the biggest fish in the whole sea. It can grow longer than **40 feet** — longer than your school bus! But it only eats tiny floaty bits, by letting water swoosh through its huge mouth."

Juno giggled. "Like a spaghetti strainer!"

"Exactly like that," said Finn.

The whale shark drifted closer, gentle and slow, speckled with white spots like stars. Milo waved instead of touching it.

"Hi, big friend," Milo said softly.

"Good job waving, not patting," Finn said. "We watch sharks. We don't touch them."

"How long do they live?" Milo asked.

"Some whale sharks live **100 years** or even more," said Finn. "Longer than your grandma and grandpa put together!"

Juno waved both hands as the giant shark swam away. "Bye, old friend!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek gray shark zoomed past, fast as a rocket.

"Ooh, that one has a pointy nose!" Milo said. "Is it a great white?"

"Good eye," said Finn. "Great whites can grow almost **20 feet** long. Watch — but only from here."

The shark opened its mouth for a yawn, showing rows of teeth shaped like little triangles.

"Whoa, ROWS?" Milo counted with his finger. "Like more than one line?"

"Yep, rows and rows," Finn said. "All those teeth help it catch slippery fish to eat. But don't worry — great whites mostly swim far away from people, and people almost never get hurt by one."

Juno hid behind Milo's arm for just a second, then peeked back out. "It's not chasing us?"

"Nope," said Finn gently. "It's busy looking for fish, not little kids."

The great white swished its tail and swam off into the blue.

"Bye, pointy-tooth friend!" Juno shouted, brave again already.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Shark with a Squished Head
chapters.text:
Something strange swam toward them: a shark with a head shaped like a hammer!

Juno burst out laughing. "Its head is SQUISHED!"

"That's a hammerhead shark," Finn said. "Its eyes sit way out on each side of that wide head."

"Why's it shaped like that?" Milo asked.

"That means it can see almost all the way around itself," Finn said. "Like having eyes in the back of your head."

Milo tried turning his head side to side like the hammerhead. "Can you see me, Juno?"

"I can see EVERYTHING!" Juno yelled, spinning in a circle.

The hammerhead swam a slow loop around them, checking them out from every angle, then flicked its tail and swam off.

"Bye, hammer-head friend!" Milo and Juno shouted together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Walking Shark
chapters.text:
Finn led them up to shallow, sparkly water near some coral.

"Look down there," Finn said.

A small spotty shark was... walking. It flip-flopped its fins like tiny paddles across the sandy bottom.

Juno's mouth fell open. "SHARKS CAN'T WALK!"

"This one can," Finn laughed. "It's called an epaulette shark. It uses its fins like little feet to walk across the reef."

Milo leaned closer. "Why would it walk instead of swim?"

"Sometimes there's barely any air in the water," Finn said. "This shark can hold on for hours with just a tiny bit, while it waddles off to find a deeper puddle."

Juno tried waddling with her arms like fins, giggling. "I'm a walking shark too!"

Milo waddled next to her, both of them flip-flopping their arms until they tipped over laughing in the bubble.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Sandpaper Skin
chapters.text:
"Can I touch a shark, just once?" Milo asked.

"You can touch the water near one," Finn said, "but not the shark itself. Here, feel this instead." Finn nudged a smooth, bumpy rock toward the bubble wall.

Milo rubbed his finger over it. "It's bumpy! Like sandpaper!"

"That's exactly what shark skin feels like," Finn said. "It's covered in teeny-tiny bumps, shaped like little teeth, that help it zoom through the water smoothly."

"Sharks have teeth on their SKIN?" Juno asked, eyes huge.

"Sort of," Finn said, grinning. "Tiny ones you'd need a magnifying glass to see."

"Sharks can feel things too," Finn added. "They feel tiny little tingles in the water, from other animals swimming nearby, through special spots on their nose."

Milo pressed his hand flat against the bubble. "Can you feel me?"

"I sure can," Finn said. "Tingle, tingle."

Juno pressed both hands too, giggling. "Tingle tingle tingle!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Shark Lady and Home
chapters.text:
A kind lady in diving gear floated into view, smiling at a shark swimming beside her like an old friend.

"That's Eugenie Clark," Finn said. "People called her the Shark Lady. She spent years and years studying sharks."

"Did she find out they're nice?" Milo asked.

"She sure did," Finn said. "She showed everyone sharks are curious, and that they can even learn tricks, like a puppy."

Juno waved. "Hi, Shark Lady!"

The Shark Lady waved back, then swam off into the blue with her shark friend close behind.

"Time to go home," Finn said softly. "You did such a good job watching, not touching, tonight."

The red brick glowed bright in Milo's pocket. **WHOOOOSH!** The ocean swirled away like bathwater down a drain.

Milo and Juno landed back on their bedroom carpet, right where they started. The old fossil tooth sat warm in Milo's hand, a little gray stone shaped just like the one they had found.

"We really went swimming with sharks," Milo whispered.

Juno yawned a giant dinosaur yawn. "Play well, sharks," she mumbled, already half asleep.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Sharks have bendy bones called **cartilage**, like the squishy part of your ear, instead of hard bones.
Sharks have been swimming in the sea for more than **400 million years**, way before dinosaurs stomped around.
A giant shark called **Megalodon** used to swim in the sea, but it is **extinct** now, which means it isn't around anymore.
We know about Megalodon mostly from its giant **fossil** teeth, hard as rock, found on the sea floor.
Sharks lose and grow **thousands of teeth** over their whole life, with new ones always moving up front.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the sea, longer than a school bus, but it only eats tiny floaty bits.
The **great white shark** can grow almost **20 feet** long and has rows and rows of pointy teeth.
The **hammerhead shark** has a wide head with eyes on each side, so it can see almost all around itself.
The **epaulette shark** can actually walk across the sea floor using its fins like little feet.
Shark skin feels bumpy like sandpaper, covered in tiny bumps shaped like teeny-tiny teeth.
A scientist named **Eugenie Clark**, called the Shark Lady, studied sharks for years and showed they are curious and can even learn tricks.

story.title: Theo and the Beautiful Game
story.subtitle: A Player One adventure through the history of soccer.

chapters.heading: Level 1: A Ball Behind a Firewall
chapters.text:
Theo was still building. Three nights of practice shots on the back patio, and now he was coding a free-kick mini-game in Roblox Studio, trying to get the ball to curve around a wall of blocks. On his monitor, a sticky-note window still glowed from last week: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD.

He hadn't deleted it. He liked it there.

Then the screen flickered green and chunky, like an old arcade cabinet waking up.

"PLAYER ONE," squeaked a small blocky shape hopping across his taskbar. Bit, his pixel guide, eight bits tall and proud of every one of them. "You built a free kick. Want to see where kicking things started?"

"Started how far back?" Theo asked.

"Try **over 2,000 years ago**," said Bit. "China. A game called **cuju**."

The room dissolved into a dusty courtyard. Men in robes dribbled a leather ball between their feet, never touching it with their hands, aiming it through a gap in a net strung between two poles.

Theo watched one guy juggle it on his knee, foot, shoulder, foot again, never letting it drop.

"That's a foot-only drill," Theo said slowly. "Like my coach's warm-up. No hands at all."

"BZZZT! Correct," said Bit. "**Cuju** is one of soccer's oldest known ancestors — basically soccer's great-great-great-grandparent."

A coin appeared in the air, pixel-gold, and dropped into Theo's palm with a satisfying CHIME.

"One per level," Bit said. "Saved games, basically."

Theo pocketed it and grinned. "Where next?"

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Game That Got Banned
chapters.text:
The courtyard dissolved into mud. Actual mud, sucking at Theo's sneakers, in a narrow medieval street packed with yelling men.

"Whoa — what is THIS?" Theo said, as a stampede of bodies crashed past him chasing an inflated pig's bladder.

"Mob football," said Bit. "No field. No ref. Sometimes whole towns played each other, one end of the street against the other."

Someone got shoved into a cart of turnips. Nobody stopped playing.

"This is basically recess with no rules," Theo said, dodging an elbow.

"King Edward the Second thought so too," said Bit. "It got so out of hand he **banned the sport in London in 1314**."

Theo laughed. "A king rage-quit soccer?"

"Pretty much."

A man barreled past carrying the ball under one arm like a running back.

Theo frowned. "That's the actual problem. There's no rule about hands. No teams. No boundaries. It's just chaos."

"So fix it," said Bit, pixel eyebrow raised.

Theo thought for a second, the way he thought through a messy Roblox Studio build. "What if you only got points for using your feet? And the street had actual edges?"

Bit's eyes flashed. "Hold that thought, Player One. Somebody's about to agree with you. Just five hundred years late."

The mud melted away. Theo held his second coin, still faintly warm.

chapters.heading: Level 3: One Rulebook to Rule Them All
chapters.text:
They landed in a wood-paneled room full of serious young men arguing over a chalkboard.

"Cambridge University, **1848**," said Bit. "Students from different schools all played football slightly differently. They sat down and wrote one shared rulebook, called the **Cambridge Rules**."

"Like patching a game so everyone's on the same version," Theo said.

"Exactly like that."

Fifteen years flicked by on a chalkboard calendar until a different room, London this time, denser with cigar smoke and stiffer collars.

"The **Football Association**," said Bit. "Founded right here, **London, October 26, 1863**."

A tall man with excellent sideburns was scribbling furiously.

"That's Ebenezer Cobb Morley," Bit said. "He personally wrote the first official **Laws of the Game** — the rulebook that's still growing today."

Morley looked up, chewing his pen. "The trouble," he muttered, "is hands. Half these clubs still want to carry the ball."

Theo stepped closer, forgetting for a second that he wasn't really there. "Ban it," he said. "No hands. Feet and head only. That's the whole game, right there."

Morley blinked at the strange boy in the strange clothes, then wrote it down anyway.

"**No player shall carry the ball,**" he read aloud.

"BZZZT! Level complete," said Bit, and the coin that dropped into Theo's hand felt heavier than the last two, like it knew it mattered.

"Did I just help write the rules of soccer?" Theo asked.

"A little," said Bit. "History's got a sense of humor."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Cup and the Scoreless Draw
chapters.text:
A roaring crowd, scarves, mud-caked boots — Theo loved this one instantly.

"The **FA Cup**," Bit announced, "first played **1871 to 1872**. Oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world."

"Like a tournament bracket," Theo said, watching teams get eliminated round by round on a chalk results board. "I built one of these for my Roblox tournament. Winner moves on, loser's out."

"You'd have fit right in," said Bit.

The scene shifted to Glasgow, wind whipping flags, two national teams lining up.

"**1872**," said Bit. "The first official international match. Scotland versus England."

Theo watched ninety minutes compress into seconds — chances missed, a shot off the post, a desperate last clearance.

The final whistle blew. The scoreboard read nothing at all.

"Zero-zero?" Theo said, almost offended. "That's the big historic match and NOBODY scored?"

"**A 0-0 draw**," Bit confirmed, grinning. "Doesn't matter. It still counts as the first one. Sometimes history's just happy somebody showed up."

Theo shook his head, laughing. "I would've been SO mad as a fan."

"They were thrilled," said Bit. "Different century, different standards."

Theo pocketed his fourth coin, still grinning at the most anticlimactic scoreboard in sports history.

chapters.heading: Level 5: Building the Servers
chapters.text:
The scene jumped forward, gaslit streets to gray industrial ones, a man pinning a schedule to a pub wall.

"William McGregor," said Bit. "**1888**. He organized the **Football League** — the first football league in the whole world."

Theo studied the schedule. Home games, away games, points for wins. It looked uncannily like the matchmaking system he'd built for his own Roblox soccer server.

"Random matches were a mess," Theo said. "You need a league table. Everybody plays everybody, fair and square."

"BZZZT. Exactly his thinking."

The wall dissolved into a grander room, flags of different countries hanging from the ceiling, seven men shaking hands around a table.

"Paris, **1904**," said Bit. "Seven countries founded **FIFA**, soccer's world office. Somebody had to run the game once it crossed borders."

"Like a global server list," Theo said, nodding slowly. "You need someone keeping all the countries' games straight."

"You keep doing that," said Bit, "turning old history into Roblox Studio. I respect it."

Theo pocketed coin number five, already smiling at coin number six waiting in Bit's outstretched pixel hand.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Ball Behind the Wall
chapters.text:
They landed inside cold stone walls, torchlit, dust floating in the air.

"Stirling Castle, Scotland," said Bit. "Somebody once found an old leather ball hidden behind these walls."

Theo crouched by a cracked display case. Inside sat a shriveled, lumpy ball, stitched by hand, nothing like the smooth ones he kicked on Saturdays.

"How old?" he asked.

"Maybe from the **1540s**," said Bit. "Which would make it the oldest football in the world."

"Maybe?" Theo repeated, eyebrow raised.

"Nobody can prove the exact year," Bit admitted. "It's a good story with some shaky homework behind it. Still — hundreds of years old, hidden in a wall, waiting to be found. That part's true."

Theo tapped the old leather gently, careful as a museum visitor. "It's wild that a ball could just sit there that long and nobody knew."

"Sort of like an old save file," said Bit, "nobody opened for centuries."

Theo grinned at that. Coin six, warm and a little dusty, dropped into his palm.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The First World Cup
chapters.text:
Sunshine, a packed stadium, a sea of flags — Uruguay, 1930.

"The very first **FIFA World Cup**," said Bit. "Thirteen teams, one host country: Uruguay."

Theo watched the host team storm down the field in the final.

"Who do they play?" he asked.

"Argentina," said Bit. "And Uruguay wins, right here, on home turf."

A roar shook the stands as the final whistle blew. A gleaming little statue was carried onto the field.

"The **Jules Rimet trophy**," Bit said, "named after the FIFA president who pushed hardest to make this whole tournament happen in the first place."

Theo studied the trophy, small enough to carry under one arm. "That's it? That's the big prize?"

"For now," said Bit, with a sly little flicker. "Keep that trophy in mind, Player One. It gets a wild story of its own."

Theo pocketed coin seven, already curious.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Trophy, The Dog, and the Win
chapters.text:
London, 1966. A glass case in an exhibition hall, the Jules Rimet trophy gleaming inside — then an alarm started SCREECHING.

"It's gone," said Bit. "Stolen right out of its case."

"Someone stole a WORLD CUP?" Theo said, delighted and horrified at once.

"For about a week," said Bit. "Then somebody's dog, sniffing around a garden hedge, found it wrapped in newspaper."

Theo scanned the grainy old footage, spotted a scruffy little dog nosing under some bushes.

"There," Theo said, pointing. "He's about to find it."

Sure enough, the dog yanked out a newspaper bundle and barked proudly.

"A dog named **Pickles** found the missing World Cup trophy," said Bit, "a week after it vanished."

"Pickles," Theo repeated, grinning. "Best name in sports history."

The scene shifted to Wembley Stadium, roaring, England's players lifting that very same trophy.

"**1966**," said Bit. "England hosted the World Cup — and won it. Still their only title."

Theo pumped a fist, coin eight landing warm in his palm, right next to the memory of a very good dog.

chapters.heading: Level 9: Three Stars and a Red Card
chapters.text:
Mexico, a scorching afternoon, a number ten weaving through defenders like they weren't there.

"**Pele**," said Bit. "Brazilian forward. The only player ever on **three** World Cup winning teams — **1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Theo watched him flick the ball over one defender's head without breaking stride. "That's not fair. That's cheat-code soccer."

"No cheat codes. Just that good."

A referee jogged past, pulling two colored cards from his pocket — one yellow, one red.

"Ken Aston," Bit explained. "A referee who got the idea from traffic lights. Yellow means slow down. Red means you're out. Debuted right here at the **1970 World Cup**."

"Like a warning system," Theo said. "We basically have that in my Roblox server — yellow warning, red kick."

"Same idea, ninety years apart," said Bit.

The scene jumped forward again. Brazil, having now won their third title, carried the little Jules Rimet trophy off for good.

"They got to keep it," said Bit, "so in **1974**, FIFA made a brand new World Cup trophy for everyone after that."

Theo caught coin number nine, already picturing a shelf of trophies back in Brazil.

chapters.heading: Level 10: Half Time For Fairness
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a packed English field, women in old-style kits lined up before a cheering crowd.

"**Lily Parr**," said Bit. "One of the best players England ever had. Her team drew bigger crowds than a lot of men's games."

Theo watched her blast a shot past the goalkeeper. "She's incredible. Why haven't I heard of her?"

Bit's voice dropped, quieter. "Because soccer's own rule-makers banned women from playing on their fields — for **fifty years**, starting not long after this."

Theo's face fell. "That's not fair. She was better than half these guys."

"You're right," said Bit simply. "It wasn't fair. But watch."

The field blurred forward through decades of women still playing anyway, parks and backyards and borrowed pitches, until finally: "**1971**. The ban got lifted."

Then one more jump — a packed stadium in China, 1991, players sprinting under bright lights.

"The first official **Women's World Cup**," said Bit. "Finally, on the biggest stage there is."

Theo watched the trophy get lifted high, grinning despite the lump in his throat. "That should've happened way sooner."

"A lot of good things should happen sooner," said Bit. "They happened anyway. That's the part worth keeping."

The tenth coin dropped into Theo's hand, and the field dissolved into pixels, then into his own bedroom ceiling.

All ten coins sat glowing in his palm. One by one they lifted, spun, and melted together into a small golden trophy, sitting right beside his keyboard.

Bit's pixel eyes went a little watery, same as always at the end of a level. "Level complete, Player One."

Theo turned the little trophy over in his hands — ten coins, ten levels, one long game nobody finished building. On his screen, a new message blinked: THE NEXT MATCH IS YOURS TO PLAY.

He thought about Saturday's game, about practicing penalties in the backyard, about a kid in China kicking a ball through a net two thousand years ago for the exact same reason he did.

Saturday couldn't come soon enough.

story.ending_line: Saturday couldn't come soon enough.

true_facts.text: **Cuju**, a kicking game played in China **over 2,000 years ago**, is one of soccer's earliest known ancestors.
Medieval street football got so wild that **King Edward II banned it in London in 1314**.
In **1848**, students at Cambridge wrote down one shared set of football rules, called the **Cambridge Rules**.
The **Football Association** was founded in **London on October 26, 1863**, and said players could not carry the ball with their hands.
**Ebenezer Cobb Morley** personally wrote the very first official rulebook for soccer in 1863.
The **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, is the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world.
The first official international match was a **0-0 draw between Scotland and England**, played in Glasgow in **1872**.
**William McGregor** started the **Football League in 1888**, the first football league in the world.
**FIFA**, the group that runs world soccer, was founded in **Paris in 1904** by seven countries.
An old leather ball found hidden at **Stirling Castle** in Scotland might date back to the **1540s**, possibly making it the oldest football in the world — though nobody's totally sure.
The first ever **World Cup** was held in **Uruguay in 1930**, and the host team beat Argentina in the final.
In **1966**, the World Cup trophy was stolen in London — then found a week later by a dog named **Pickles**.
Brazilian forward **Pele** is the only player ever to win **three World Cups**: **1958, 1962, and 1970**.
Women's football was banned in England for **fifty years** before the ban was finally lifted in **1971**.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Ten golden coins fuse into a small trophy beside Theo's keyboard, and his screen blinks THE NEXT MATCH IS YOURS TO PLAY as he thinks ahead to Saturday's game.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Hotspot Brick
story.subtitle: A glowing LEGO brick takes three kids deep inside Earth's fieriest mountains.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo stacked his LEGO bricks into a tall, wobbly mountain. Juno walked her toy dinosaur, Spike, up the plastic slope. Theo bounced his soccer ball softly off the wall. Bonk. Bonk. Bonk.

Then the top brick began to glow orange. It started to HUM, low and rumbly, like a drum.

"Guys," Milo whispered. "My brick is doing something weird."

The glow spread across the carpet. The carpet rippled like water. A warm, orange tunnel opened right where the mountain used to be.

"COOL!" shouted Theo.

Juno grabbed Spike. "Dinosaur wants to go too!"

WHOOOOSH! Down they slid, through the glowing tunnel, spinning and giggling, straight toward the middle of the Earth.

They landed with a soft thump on warm red rock. A real mountain stood in front of them, spitting orange goo high into the sky.

"Whoa," said Milo. "Is that a volcano?"

The glowing brick floated up and turned into a tiny light, like a firefly made of fire. "That's right," it said. "I'm Hotspot, your very own volcano guide. A **volcano** is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock escapes."

"What's the orange goo?" asked Juno, pointing with her whole arm.

"Underground we call it **magma**," said Hotspot. "Once it comes out where we can see it, we call it **lava**."

Theo watched a glowing glob ooze slowly down the mountain. "It's so slow. Like a cheese fountain at a party."

Milo snorted with laughter. "Lava cheese fountain!"

Juno giggled so hard she nearly dropped Spike. She waved him near the warm rock, careful not to get too close.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Shaky Puzzle Pieces
chapters.text:
Hotspot's glow brightened like a happy little sun. "Ready to fly?"

Up they zoomed, high above the ground, wind tickling their cheeks.

"Look down," said Hotspot. "The ground is made of giant puzzle pieces called **plates**. They float, and bump, ever so slowly, slower than a snail."

Theo squinted at the shapes below. "Is that why some places get more volcanoes than others?"

"Exactly," said Hotspot. "Most volcanoes grow right where puzzle pieces push together, pull apart, or slide past each other."

A huge curved line of glowing dots circled the ocean below, like a sparkly necklace.

Milo gasped. "Is that a giant horseshoe?"

"We call it the **Ring of Fire**," said Hotspot. "It goes almost all the way around this whole ocean. About three out of every four awake volcanoes on Earth live right there."

Juno counted the dots with her finger, bouncing in the air. "One, two, three... dino-lots!"

Everyone laughed. Theo gave Juno a high five, and Milo pretended his LEGO brick was a tiny volcano on the necklace too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Volcano Island Country
chapters.text:
Hotspot zoomed them down toward a long line of green islands, poking up out of blue water.

"Welcome to Indonesia," said Hotspot. "Theo, want to count the mountains?"

Theo counted smoking peaks popping up one after another, faster and faster. "One, two, five, ten... there's SO many!"

"This country has more awake volcanoes than any other place on Earth," said Hotspot.

Milo tried picturing it all in LEGO bricks. "I'd need a hundred bricks just for the mountains!"

A soft puff of white smoke rose from one peak, like a sleepy sigh after a long nap.

Juno patted Spike's head. "Dino says that's a lot of fire mountains."

"It sure is," said Hotspot, smiling his tiny glowing smile.

Theo wiped his forehead. "My arms are tired from counting."

Milo laughed. "That's because you used all ten fingers twice!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Hawaii's Hot Spot
chapters.text:
They landed on black, bumpy rock in the middle of a wide blue ocean.

"This is Hawaii," said Hotspot. "It didn't grow at a puzzle-piece edge. It grew over a **hotspot**, a super-hot spot deep underground that keeps pushing melted rock up, up, up."

Milo noticed the mountain nearby was wide and gently sloped, nothing like the pointy mountains he'd seen before. "It's not pointy like a party-hat mountain. It's flat and wide!"

"Good eye," said Hotspot. "Some volcanoes are wide and gentle, like this one. Others are tall and pointy, like Japan's Mount Fuji."

Orange lava glowed and bubbled nearby. Plip. Plip. Plip. "This one is **Kilauea**," said Hotspot. "It has been bubbling and glowing, on and off, for a very long time."

Theo pointed at an even bigger mountain beside it. "And that one?"

"**Mauna Loa**," said Hotspot. "It's the biggest volcano on Earth. Taller than **4,000 meters** — that's super duper tall."

Juno stretched Spike's little arms as wide as they could go. "Biggest ever, like a dino!"

Milo grinned. "I'm building this one when we get home. Shark included, probably."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Brand New Island
chapters.text:
Hotspot flew them north, where the air turned chilly and the ocean turned gray.

"Brrr," said Theo, rubbing his arms. "Where's this?"

"**Iceland**," said Hotspot. "Here, the puzzle pieces under the ground are pulling apart instead of pushing together."

Below the waves, bubbles fizzed and popped. FIZZ. POP. SPLOOSH!

"Something's happening!" shouted Milo, pointing at the sea.

Steam shot up from the water. Black rock piled higher and higher, right in front of their eyes.

"In **1963**, this exact thing happened," said Hotspot. "A brand new island popped right up out of the ocean, out of nowhere. They named it **Surtsey**."

Juno's eyes went huge. "A whole new island? From bubbles?"

"From volcano bubbles," said Hotspot, smiling.

Theo nodded slowly, very impressed. "That's the coolest level-up I've ever seen."

Milo peered closer. "Can we visit it?"

"Not today," said Hotspot gently. "It's still very new, and still a little hot."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Sleepy Giant
chapters.text:
They landed in a steamy meadow full of colorful, bubbling pools — blue, orange, and green.

"This is Yellowstone," said Hotspot. "Under this whole park sleeps a giant volcano called a **supervolcano**."

Juno hid behind Milo's leg. "Is it going to wake up?"

Hotspot's light glowed warm and steady, not scary at all. "No, don't worry. Its last big eruption was about **640,000 years ago**. Scientists watch it every single day. They see no sign it's waking up soon."

Juno peeked back out. "Phew!"

Theo grinned. "So it's basically sleeping on easy mode."

Milo held up a LEGO brick like it was the sleepy mountain. "Shhh. Don't wake it."

Everyone tiptoed past a bubbling pool, giggling the whole way, careful not to splash.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Biggest Volcano Ever
chapters.text:
Hotspot's light turned silvery, like moonlight. "Ready for somewhere really, really far away?"

WHOOOOSH! They zoomed past the moon, straight to a red, dusty planet.

"This is Mars," said Hotspot. "And that mountain is **Olympus Mons**."

Theo tipped his head back, and back, and back. "That cannot be real. How tall even is that?"

"About **thirteen and a half miles** high," said Hotspot. "Almost three Mount Everests stacked on top of each other."

Milo's jaw dropped all the way open. "That's bigger than any LEGO tower I've ever built. Bigger than any tower anyone's ever built!"

Juno held Spike up toward the mountain. "Even bigger than a dinosaur!"

"The biggest volcano anyone has ever found," said Hotspot proudly. "Anywhere in the whole solar system."

Theo tried to imagine climbing it in a game. "That would take, like, a hundred levels."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Rug
chapters.text:
Hotspot's glow dimmed to a cozy orange, like a nightlight.

"One more secret before bed," said Hotspot. "Scientists who study volcanoes use special machines. These machines feel tiny shakes in the ground, shakes too small for us to even notice. They also have machines flying way up in the sky. Those watch for the ground puffing up, like a balloon. Both kinds help scientists know if a volcano might wake up soon."

Milo nodded, like it made total sense. "So they're basically keeping watch, like goalies guarding a net."

"And when ash falls and settles," Hotspot added, "it turns into some of the best dirt for growing yummy plants. That's why farmers like living near volcanoes, even though they're careful."

Juno yawned a dino-sized yawn. "Can Spike grow a volcano garden?"

"Maybe a tiny one," laughed Hotspot.

The orange tunnel opened again. WHOOOOSH! Down, down, down, and THUMP, they landed back on the soft carpet, right where they started.

The LEGO mountain stood exactly where Milo had left it. But now, right on top, sat one tiny, glowing brick. It felt warm, like it remembered everything.

Milo picked it up gently and set it on his shelf. "Goodnight, Hotspot."

Juno hugged Spike close. Theo set his soccer ball down by the door, yawning too.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Sleep well, little volcano watchers.

true_facts.text: A **volcano** is a hole in the ground where hot melted rock can escape.
Underground the hot rock is called **magma**; once it flows out, we call it **lava**.
Most volcanoes grow where Earth's giant puzzle pieces, called **plates**, push, pull, or slide past each other.
The **Ring of Fire** is a giant horseshoe around the ocean where about three out of every four of Earth's volcanoes live.
**Indonesia** has more volcanoes than any other country on Earth.
Hawaii's volcanoes grew over a **hotspot**, a super-hot spot deep underground, not where puzzle pieces meet.
**Kilauea** in Hawaii has been bubbling and glowing on and off for a very long time.
**Mauna Loa** in Hawaii is the biggest volcano on Earth, taller than **4,000 meters**.
In **1963**, a brand new island called **Surtsey** popped right up out of the ocean near Iceland.
In Iceland, the puzzle pieces under the ground are pulling apart instead of pushing together.
Under **Yellowstone** sleeps a giant volcano called a **supervolcano**. Its last big eruption was about **640,000 years ago**, and scientists see no sign it will wake up soon.
**Olympus Mons** on Mars is the biggest volcano ever found — about **thirteen and a half miles** high, almost **three Mount Everests** stacked up.
Scientists use special machines to feel tiny shakes in the ground, and machines in the sky to watch for the ground puffing up, to see if a volcano might wake up.
Ash from volcanoes turns into some of the best dirt for growing plants, which is why farmers like living nearby.

story.title: Juno and the Buzzy Bee Adventure
story.subtitle: A tiny glowing bee takes Juno back to meet the busiest family in the world.

chapters.heading: Chapter One: The Buzzy Spot
chapters.text:
Juno lined up her dinosaur toys on the rug. Stomp, stomp, went her toy stegosaurus. It was way past bedtime, but she wasn't tired yet.

Then one yellow spot on the stegosaurus's back began to glow. It buzzed, soft and low. BZZZZZ.

A tiny bee popped out of the glow. "Hello, Juno!" she said. "I'm Buzz!"

Juno blinked. "Bees don't glow," she said.

"This one does," said Buzz, wiggling her wings. "Want to see where bees lived a long, long time ago? Even with dinosaurs?"

Juno grabbed her stegosaurus. "YES!"

Buzz spun around her, and the rug melted into green leaves and ferns.

chapters.heading: Chapter Two: Bees and Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
A big dinosaur thumped by, far away. Juno gasped.

"Bees really lived with dinosaurs?" she asked.

"They sure did," said Buzz. She pointed to a blob of golden tree goo, hard and shiny like candy.

"Long ago, a bee got stuck in goo like this," said Buzz. "It turned hard, like a see-through rock, and kept the bee safe inside forever. We call that **amber**."

"That was **a hundred million years ago**," Buzz added. "Older than your grandma!"

Juno giggled. "That's REALLY old."

She patted her stegosaurus. "Bees and dinosaurs. Friends!"

chapters.heading: Chapter Three: The Busy Hive
chapters.text:
Buzz flew Juno to a hive, humming like a tiny city.

"Who's in charge?" asked Juno.

"The **queen bee**," said Buzz. "She's the busiest mom here."

Juno peeked inside. Rows and rows of tiny white eggs filled the little rooms.

"She lays up to **two thousand eggs** every day," said Buzz.

Juno counted on her fingers and gave up at ten. "That's SO many!"

"And a hive can hold **up to eighty thousand bees** in summer," Buzz said.

Juno spread her arms wide. "Like a whole dinosaur's worth of bees!"

Buzz laughed. "Close enough."

chapters.heading: Chapter Four: Everybody Has a Job
chapters.text:
Bees zoomed past, each one busy.

"What do they all do?" Juno asked.

"Every **worker bee** is a girl," said Buzz, "and they take turns doing every job."

Juno watched one bee sweeping a little room clean. Another stood by the front door, buzzing at nothing.

"That one's a guard!" Juno said, pointing. "She's keeping watch!"

"Good eye," said Buzz. "Tomorrow, she might fly off to find flowers instead."

Juno nodded slowly. "Everybody gets a turn being everything."

"Exactly," said Buzz. "Nobody's stuck doing one boring job forever."

chapters.heading: Chapter Five: The Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
One bee landed and started to wiggle.

"Why is she dancing?" Juno asked.

"She's telling her sisters where the flowers are," said Buzz. "It's called the **waggle dance**. Wiggle this way means flowers are that way!"

"I can wiggle too!" Juno jumped up and waggled toward her stegosaurus. "Flowers are THAT way!"

The real bees buzzed closer, checking her dance.

"Not bad," said Buzz, giggling. "A scientist named **Karl** figured this dance out, just by watching bees."

Juno waggled again, prouder this time.

chapters.heading: Chapter Six: Flower Hunting
chapters.text:
Buzz led Juno to a field, buzzing with wings.

"Bees have **five eyes**," said Buzz. "Two big ones for shapes and colors, and three tiny ones on top for sunshine."

Juno tried to count her own eyes. "I only have two!"

"That's plenty for you," laughed Buzz.

A bee landed on a flower and sipped its sweet juice, called **nectar**.

"Her wings flap **two hundred times every second**," said Buzz. "That's the buzzing sound you hear!"

Juno flapped her arms as fast as she could. She got nowhere close.

"Worth a try," said Buzz.

chapters.heading: Chapter Seven: Making Honey
chapters.text:
Back at the hive, bees poured nectar into little rooms with six sides.

"Why are the rooms six-sided?" Juno asked, tracing the shape with her finger.

"We call that a **hexagon**," said Buzz. "It holds the most honey using the least wax. Clever, right?"

"One bee only makes a tiny, tiny bit of honey her whole life," Buzz said, "smaller than a drop from your juice cup."

"Then how do they make so much?" Juno asked.

"Bees visit about **two million flowers** together," said Buzz, "just to fill one jar."

Juno's eyes went wide. "TEAMWORK!"

chapters.heading: Chapter Eight: Honey Forever
chapters.text:
Buzz showed Juno an old clay pot of honey.

"People in **Egypt** kept bees and gathered honey a very, very long time ago," said Buzz. "Some honey from back then was found **still good to eat**!"

"Honey never goes bad?" Juno asked.

"Hardly ever," said Buzz. "It's an amazing, forever treat."

Juno hugged her stegosaurus. "Dinosaurs never got to try honey."

"Maybe not," laughed Buzz, "but you did."

The glow faded. Juno blinked, back on her rug, toys all around.

On her stegosaurus sat one tiny golden sticker, shaped like a hexagon.

Juno smiled and closed her eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Buzz well.

true_facts.text: A long, long time ago, bees lived with dinosaurs — some got stuck in sticky tree goo that turned hard like glass, called **amber**.
A bee family has one **queen bee** and lots of worker bees.
The queen bee can lay up to **two thousand eggs** every day.
A hive can hold up to **eighty thousand bees** in summer.
Every **worker bee** is a girl, and they take turns doing every job in the hive.
Bees do a wiggly **waggle dance** to tell each other where the flowers are.
A bee has **five eyes** — two big ones and three tiny ones on top.
A bee's wings flap **two hundred times every second**, which makes the buzzing sound.
Bees visit about **two million flowers** together just to make one jar of honey.
One bee makes only a tiny drop of honey in her whole life.
Honeycomb rooms are shaped like a six-sided **hexagon**, so bees store lots of honey using only a little wax.
Honey lasts so long that old honey from **Egypt** was found still good to eat.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Juno returned to her rug to find a tiny golden hexagon sticker left on her stegosaurus toy by Buzz the Bee.
