story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Terrible Lizards
story.subtitle: A sleepy trip back to the very first dinosaurs

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping tiny LEGO teeth onto a grey LEGO shark.

Juno sat next to him, lining up her dinosaur toys in a wiggly row. "RAWR!" she said, for the hundredth time.

It had been one whole week since their giant LEGO tower went **CLICK** and stayed standing. Now the little red brick sat quiet on the shelf.

Then it started to glow.

"Milo," Juno whispered. "It's doing the thing."

The red brick pulsed, bright as a stoplight. It gave one happy **CLICK**.

"Here we go," Milo grinned, grabbing Juno's hand.

**WHOOOOSH!**

The bedroom spun into green and brown. When it stopped, Milo and Juno stood in warm mud, under a strange sky.

Something small and scaly peeked out from a fern. It had big eyes and little claws.

"Hello!" it chirped. "I'm Sprout. Want to meet the very first dinosaurs?"

Juno gasped. "YES!"

Sprout hopped onto a rock. "Dinosaurs first showed up about **230 million years ago**," she said. "That's so long ago, nobody you know was even born yet. Not your mommy. Not your mommy's mommy."

Milo looked at the little lizard-like creatures darting past his sneakers. "They're tiny," he said. "I thought dinosaurs were huge!"

"Not yet," said Sprout. "Some stayed small. Some grew HUGE. You'll see."

Milo counted five little dinosaurs scurrying between rocks. "One, two, three, four, five!"

Sprout clicked her claws, happy. "Good counting! Want to find out what the word *dinosaur* even means?"

Juno jumped up. "YEAH!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Terrible Lizard
chapters.text:
A sign made of carved stone stood in a clearing. Sprout led them to it. Letters were scratched all over it.

"Nobody could read this for a long, long time," said Sprout. "Then one person figured it out."

Milo traced the carved letters with his finger. "D...I...N...O," he sounded out.

"That's close!" said Sprout. "A man named **Richard Owen** looked at old dinosaur bones. In **1842**, he gave this whole group of animals a brand new name."

"What name?" asked Juno, bouncing on her toes.

"Dinosaur," said Sprout. "It means **'terrible lizard'** in a very old language."

Milo scrunched his nose. "Terrible? Like, naughty?"

"More like 'fierce,'" said Sprout. "Big and scary-looking. Not naughty."

Juno put her hands up like claws. "I'm a terrible lizard!" she roared.

Milo laughed so hard he nearly slipped in the mud. "You're a terrible dinosaur, maybe."

Sprout giggled, a little chirpy sound. "Close enough!"

The carved sign began to glow the same red as Milo's brick. Milo touched it gently.

"Can we see a real one?" he asked. "A big one?"

Sprout's eyes sparkled. "I know exactly who to show you. Follow the glowing footprints."

Giant footprints, each one glowing faintly red, led off into the trees. Juno hopped from one to the next like stepping stones.

"This one's bigger than my whole bed!" she shouted.
chapters.shout_line: THIS ONE'S BIGGER THAN MY WHOLE BED!

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Teeth Like Rulers
chapters.text:
The footprints stopped at a clearing. Something huge was eating behind a wall of trees. Crunch. Crunch. CRUNCH.

Juno froze. "Is it scary?"

Sprout patted her shoulder with a tiny wing. "She's just hungry. And she's friendly to visitors who stay back and watch."

A giant dinosaur stepped out. Her head was as big as a car. Her arms were tiny, but her mouth was enormous.

"That's a **T. rex**," whispered Milo, eyes wide.

"Her teeth," said Sprout, "could grow up to **twelve inches long**. That's as long as a school ruler, counting the part stuck inside the gum too."

Milo held up his LEGO shark, comparing it to the dinosaur's mouth. "Whoa. A shark tooth is tiny next to that!"

Juno peeked out from behind Sprout. "Does she bite kids?"

"No," said Sprout gently. "She's busy eating a plant-muncher who already wandered off. We're just watching, from far away, like at the zoo."

The T. rex let out a huge, rumbly ROAR. Juno jumped — then giggled.

"She sounds like my tummy when I'm hungry for pancakes," Juno said.

Milo cracked up. "Pancake Rex!"

Sprout snorted a laugh so big a puff of ferns blew sideways.

The T. rex wandered off into the trees, tail swishing, not bothered by them one bit.

"Where to next?" Milo asked, tucking his shark LEGO back in his pocket.

Sprout pointed at a rustle in the bushes. "Something small is hiding right there. Wanna guess what it is?"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Turkey, Not Monster
chapters.text:
The bushes rustled again. Milo crept closer, careful not to scare it.

"In movies," Milo said, "raptors are as big as me!"

Sprout shook her head, smiling. "Real **Velociraptors** were only about the size of a turkey."

Out popped a small, feathery dinosaur, no taller than Juno's knee. It tilted its head, curious.

Juno laughed. "That's not scary! It's cute!"

"Look closer," said Sprout. "What do you notice on its arms?"

Milo leaned in. "Feathers! It has feathers, like a bird!"

"Good eye," said Sprout. "Lots of dinosaurs had feathers. People found out by studying old bones very closely."

Juno reached her hand out, and Sprout gently stopped her. "We watch with our eyes, not our hands. Even friendly dinosaurs like their space."

Juno nodded and waved instead. "Hi, feather dinosaur!"

The little dinosaur chirped back, almost like a sparrow.

Milo tilted his head. "Wait. Feathers... and it chirps... Sprout, is it kind of like a bird?"

Sprout clapped her claws. "You're onto something big, Milo. Hold that thought for later."

The feathery dinosaur scampered off between the ferns, quick as a kitten.

Juno spun in a circle. "I wanna chirp like a dino-bird!" She let out a wobbly chirp-roar.

Milo cracked up. "That was NOT a chirp."

"It was a Juno-chirp," she said proudly.

Sprout led them onward, following a trail of giant, armored footprints. "Next up," she said, "some dinosaurs with the best armor you've ever seen."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Plates, Spikes, and Horns
chapters.text:
The trail opened into a sunny meadow. A dinosaur with big bony plates down its back munched on leaves.

"Whoa," breathed Milo. "It looks like it's wearing armor!"

"That's a **Stegosaurus**," said Sprout. "Those plates run all along her back. See her tail?"

Juno squinted. "It has pointy spikes!"

"Exactly," said Sprout. "Sharp spikes on the end of her tail, for swinging at anyone who bothers her."

Milo pretended to swing an imaginary tail. "SWISH! Stay back!"

Juno copied him, wiggling her bottom like a tail. "SWISH SWISH!"

Across the meadow, another dinosaur lifted its head. It had three horns and a big bony frill, like a shield, behind its head.

"That's a **Triceratops**," said Sprout. "Three horns on its face, and that big frill protects its neck."

Juno counted the horns on her fingers. "One, two, three! Three horns!"

"Perfect counting again," said Sprout.

Milo studied the two dinosaurs grazing peacefully, side by side. "They're not fighting each other," he said.

"Nope," said Sprout. "Plant-eaters mostly just want their leaves. The spikes and horns keep them safe from hungry dinosaurs, like our pancake-loving friend from before."

Juno giggled. "Pancake Rex better stay away!"

The Triceratops gave a low snort, almost like a hello. Juno waved both hands back.

"Can we build one?" Milo asked, patting his pocket where spare LEGO pieces jingled.

Sprout's eyes twinkled. "First, let's find out how we even know what dinosaurs looked like at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Bones Turned to Stone
chapters.text:
Sprout led them to a rocky cliff by the sea. Waves crashed below.

"This is where people find dinosaur clues, even in your own time," said Sprout.

"Clues?" asked Juno.

"**Fossils**," said Sprout. "A fossil is old bones that turned hard like stone, after being buried a long, long time."

Milo knelt and brushed dirt off a shape in the rock. A curved bone peeked out.

"I found one!" he shouted.

"You sure did," said Sprout. "People who study fossils for a job are called **paleontologists**. It's a big word for 'bone detectives.'"

Juno tried the word. "Pay-lee-on-tol-o-gist!" She beamed. "I said it!"

"A long time ago," said Sprout, "a girl named **Mary Anning** hunted for fossils on beaches just like this one. She found amazing sea creatures from dinosaur times."

"A girl my age?" asked Milo.

"Older than you, but still young," said Sprout. "Brave, too. She was always careful on the cliffs."

"Some people tell a story," Sprout added, "about a farmer's dog that supposedly dug up part of a famous dinosaur. It's a fun tale — but nobody's really sure it's true. More of a tall tale than real history."

Juno giggled. "A digging dog!"

Milo gently lifted his bone-shaped fossil and held it up to the light. "Can we keep looking?"

Sprout nodded. "Let's go see one of the most famous dinosaur bone-sets ever dug up."

"Let's go!" said Juno, already running.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Sue
chapters.text:
The ground rippled with the same warm glow as Milo's brick. When it cleared, they stood inside a giant room, full of enormous bones standing tall.

"Whoa," whispered Milo. "It's HUGE."

"This is **Sue**," said Sprout. "One of the biggest, most complete T. rex bone-sets ever found. People dug her up in **South Dakota** in **1990**."

Juno tipped her head all the way back, looking up at the skull. "That's higher than my whole house!"

Milo walked slowly around the bones, counting the ribs. "One, two, three..." He lost count at ten and laughed. "So many!"

"Why's she called Sue?" asked Juno.

"Named after the person who found her," said Sprout. "People who search for fossils often name their big finds."

Milo tapped his chin, thinking hard. "If I found a dinosaur, I'd name it Shark-o-saurus."

Juno gasped. "I'd name mine Juno-rex!"

Sprout laughed so hard her feathers puffed up. "Both excellent names."

Milo set his LEGO shark gently on the ground beside Sue's enormous stone foot, just to compare sizes.

"My shark is basically a crumb," Milo said, grinning.

Juno held her hand near one of Sue's giant toe bones, careful not to touch the real one. "Her toes are bigger than my whole hand!"

The red brick in Milo's pocket pulsed warmly, like it was proud of them.

"One more stop," said Sprout. "I want to show you something that might surprise you both."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Ones Who Stayed
chapters.text:
Sprout led them outside, to a tree full of chirping birds.

"Remember that little feathery dinosaur from before?" Sprout asked. "The one that chirped like a sparrow?"

Milo's eyes went wide. "Yeah!"

"Birds today," said Sprout, "came from dinosaurs just like that one. So really, dinosaurs never totally went away. Some of them turned into birds, and birds are still here, every single day."

Juno looked up at the chirping tree, delighted. "The birds outside my window... are dinosaurs?!"

"Sort of!" said Sprout, smiling. "Pretty amazing, right?"

Milo frowned a little. "But what happened to the really big ones? The T. rex and the Triceratops?"

Sprout's voice stayed gentle. "A long, long time ago, about **66 million years ago**, something big changed on Earth. Most of the huge dinosaurs couldn't live through it, and they went away."

Juno's lip wobbled, just a little. "All of them?"

"Not all," said Sprout, squeezing her small claw around Juno's hand. "The feathery ones — the bird ones — made it through. That's why we still have birds singing outside every single morning."

Juno looked back up at the chirping tree, and her wobble turned into a smile. "Hi, dino-birds!"

Milo smiled too. "So dinosaurs are kind of still everywhere. We just didn't know it."

"Exactly," said Sprout. "Pretty neat way for a story to keep going, huh?"

The red brick in Milo's pocket began to glow brighter and brighter, humming warmly.

"I think that means it's time to go home," said Milo.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
Sprout walked them to a soft patch of ferns, glowing gently like a nightlight.

"Thanks for showing us everything," said Milo, giving Sprout a gentle, careful pat.

"Thanks for finding things, and counting things, and asking such good questions," said Sprout. "Come back and visit soon."

Juno waved, careful like she'd learned. "Bye, feather friend!"

The red brick glowed its brightest red yet. It gave one giant, happy **CLICK**.

**WHOOOOSH!**

The green and brown spun into pink and beige — their own bedroom carpet. Milo and Juno landed softly, right where they'd started.

On the carpet between them sat something new: a tiny LEGO dinosaur, plates on its back, three little horns, feathers along one arm, all snapped together from spare bricks.

"Did we build that?" Milo asked, blinking.

Juno picked it up carefully. "Sprout must have left it!"

Milo turned the little LEGO dinosaur over in his hands. "Terrible lizard," he whispered, smiling. "But not so terrible."

Juno yawned a huge yawn, her dinosaur toys scattered all around her like old friends. "Birds are dinosaurs," she mumbled sleepily. "Cool."

The red brick on the shelf gave one last, soft pulse, then went quiet and dark, just like always.

Milo tucked the new LEGO dinosaur onto the windowsill, right where he could see it first thing in the morning.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Dinosaurs first showed up about **230 million years ago**.
A man named **Richard Owen** gave dinosaurs their name in **1842**.
The word dinosaur means **'terrible lizard.'**
A **T. rex**'s teeth could grow up to **twelve inches long**.
A real **Velociraptor** was only about the size of a turkey.
Many dinosaurs, including that little raptor, had **feathers**.
Birds today came from feathery dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never totally went away.
A **Stegosaurus** had bony plates on its back and sharp spikes on its tail.
A **Triceratops** had three horns and a big bony frill.
A **fossil** is old bones that turned hard like stone after being buried a long time.
People who study fossils for a job are called **paleontologists**.
**Sue**, one of the biggest T. rex bone-sets ever found, was dug up in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
Most of the huge dinosaurs went away about **66 million years ago**, but the feathery ones became today's birds.
A story about a farmer's dog digging up a dinosaur bone is probably just a fun tall tale.

new_recurring.name: Sprout
new_recurring.rule: A small, friendly feathered dinosaur who appears whenever the magic red brick opens a history or science adventure; she greets the children warmly, explains facts in simple words, and always reminds them to watch animals gently, with eyes…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno land back on their bedroom carpet to find a tiny LEGO dinosaur with plates, horns, and feathers left behind by their new guide Sprout, and the red brick goes quiet on the shelf until next time.

scenarios.why: #48: A15 cell. A child who loves spiders and geckos: rule 10 - wild animals are watched, never touched.
scenarios.best_moment: "Gross," said Sam happily. He loved gross.
scenarios.worst_moment: It was Sam's new spider friend, still swinging gently on its silk thread.
editor_notes: Fix the Chapter 2/3 seam. Either retitle Ch3 (the spider isn't Webster) or cut the repeated 'It was Sam's new spider friend' opener, so the new spider is introduced once, cleanly.

Plant 'Climb high, stick tight' early and repeat it as a shout-along at each chapter end. Then the final line pays off a refrain the child has been chanting, and the story gains about 150-200 words toward the target range.

Link the scenes with a small reason to move on (Tokay scurrying along a wall, or following a creature) instead of 'The wall outside turned into a cliff'. Also add the bat-claw fact to the True Facts list.

story.title: Sam and the Climbing Club
story.subtitle: A sticky, stretchy bedtime adventure about how animals climb walls

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor with his flashlight.

Inside a jar next to him sat Webster, a little brown spider he had caught in the garden that very afternoon. Sam loved spiders. He loved geckos too. He loved pretty much every bug that ever crawled across his shoe.

On the shelf above his bed sat Tokay, his glow-in-the-dark gecko night light. Every night, Tokay just glowed green and stayed still.

Not tonight.

Tonight, Tokay blinked. Once. Twice. Three times.

Then, very slowly, Tokay peeled one little plastic foot off the wall — the exact same way a real gecko peels its foot, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.

"Evening, Sam," said Tokay, in a voice like a happy whisper.

Sam sat straight up. "You can TALK?"

"I can talk," said Tokay, "and I can climb. Want to know my secret?"

Sam nodded so hard his hair flopped.

"My toes," said Tokay, "have millions of **tiny hairs**, so small you can't even see them. That's how I run up glass and walk across your ceiling without falling."

Sam pressed his own hand flat on the wall and pushed. Nothing happened. He slid right down with a soft *thud* onto his bottom.

Tokay laughed, a tiny squeaky laugh. "You need gecko toes for that trick."

"Can I get some?" Sam asked.

"Better," said Tokay. "Let's go see them up close."

Tokay's eyes flashed bright green. The room spun. Sam felt himself shrink down, down, down, smaller than Webster's jar, smaller than a bug.

**WHOOOOSH!**

When the spinning stopped, Sam was standing on a gecko's giant toe.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tiny Hug
chapters.text:
The toe under Sam's feet looked like a soft, bumpy hill.

"Whoa," Sam whispered. "It's not even sticky. It's just... fuzzy."

"Good eye," said Tokay, scurrying up beside him. "Those tiny hairs split into even tinier tips. They get SO close to the wall that they just hold on — like a soft, gentle **hug**. No glue at all."

Sam reached out and touched the wall himself. His finger did not stick one bit.

"That's because you're not a gecko," said Tokay. "But here — watch this part. It's the best bit."

Tokay walked across the glass, upside down, cool as anything. Then, one toe at a time, he peeled his feet up. *Peel. Peel. Peel.*

"See?" said Tokay. "My feet never get sticky or gross, because it isn't glue. I can lift off any time I want, nice and easy."

Sam gasped. "So you could walk on my ceiling and never get stuck forever?"

"Never forever," Tokay agreed. "Just until I feel like coming down."

Sam tried peeling his own fingers off the glass like Tokay did, lifting one at a time, humming to himself. He wobbled. He giggled. He did not stick even a little.

"Worth a try," said Tokay kindly.

Suddenly, something small and eight-legged dropped down on a thread right next to Sam's ear.

Sam spun around. "WEBSTER?!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Webster's Secret
chapters.text:
It was not Webster. It was a different spider, swinging gently on its silk thread.

"Spiders live here too," said Tokay. "Go ahead and ask her your question, Sam. I know you've got one."

Sam grinned. He always had a spider question. "How do YOU climb glass?" he asked.

The spider lifted one leg and wiggled it. Sam leaned in close. Thousands of tiny hairs covered her foot, just like Tokay's.

"Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too," said Tokay. "That's how so many spiders can climb straight up glass, same as me."

"Webster has those!" Sam shouted. "I knew it!"

Just then, a fly buzzed past and landed on the wall with a tiny *bonk*.

"Different trick," said Tokay, pointing. "Flies and some beetles have little pads that drip out sticky goo, like **tiny drops of glue**. Squish, stick, climb."

Sam watched the fly's feet leave little shiny dots on the glass as it walked.

"Gross," said Sam happily. He loved gross.

"Different bugs, different tricks," said Tokay. "Hairs. Glue drops. There's more ahead. Follow me — and Sam? Remember, we look, we don't grab."

Sam nodded. He really did want to scoop up that spider. He kept his hands in his pockets instead, proud of himself.

"Good climber," said Tokay, and they scurried on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Ants with Two Tools
chapters.text:
A line of ants marched past, straight up a rough brick wall.

"Watch their feet," said Tokay.

Sam squinted. The ants' feet had tiny sharp hooks, like teeny claws, that grabbed onto every little bump in the brick.

Then the ants reached a smooth window and something changed. Out popped sticky little pads instead.

"Ants and cockroaches carry **two tools**," said Tokay. "Sharp claws for bumpy walls. Sticky pads for smooth ones. They swap, depending on the wall."

"Like how I wear boots in the rain and sneakers when it's sunny!" said Sam.

"Exactly like that," said Tokay, impressed.

Up ahead, the path split. One way led to a rough, bumpy rock. The other led to smooth, shiny glass.

"Which tool would the ant need for THAT one?" Tokay asked, pointing at the rock.

Sam thought hard. "Claws! Because it's bumpy!"

An ant marched by right on cue, claws out, and climbed the rock perfectly.

"Nailed it," said Tokay.

Sam puffed out his chest. He was basically an ant expert now.

"What about the glass one?" Tokay asked.

"Sticky pads!" Sam shouted.

Another ant zipped past and proved him right, gluing its way right up the window.

"Two for two," said Tokay. "Nice work, Climbing Club."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Goat on the Cliff
chapters.text:
The wall outside turned into a towering rocky cliff.

Sam looked way, way up. "Is that too high?" he asked, just a little wobbly.

"Not for him," said Tokay, pointing.

A mountain goat stood near the very top, calm as could be, hopping from rock to rock.

"How does he not fall?" Sam asked.

"His hooves," said Tokay. "They have a hard edge on the outside, and a soft, squishy middle that molds right around the rock, like a tiny glove."

The goat hopped down a bit further, proving it, never slipping once.

"He's totally fine," said Tokay. "Goats climb cliffs like this every day."

Sam breathed out. Good. He liked that.

A flash of fur zipped past them up a nearby tree trunk.

"Squirrel!" Sam yelled.

"Different climber, different tool," said Tokay. "Squirrels use sharp, curved **claws** that dig into teeny cracks you and I can't even see."

Sam watched the squirrel zoom straight up, no slipping, no sliding.

"Goat hooves for rock. Squirrel claws for tree bark," said Tokay. "Pick the wrong tool, and —"

He wiggled his hand and made a silly *sploosh* sound, like someone slipping into a puddle.

Sam cracked up laughing. "Wrong shoes for the rain!"

"Exactly," said Tokay, grinning his little gecko grin.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Frogs and Slow Snails
chapters.text:
Rain began to patter on giant leaves above them.

"Perfect," said Tokay. "Now you'll see my favorite wet-weather climbers."

A little green tree frog hopped onto a leaf and stuck there, upside down, not sliding one bit.

Sam leaned in close. The frog's toes were flat, with a pattern like tiny **honeycombs**.

"Tree frogs have special sticky toe pads," said Tokay, "shaped just like that, to help them grip wet leaves and even wet glass."

"Honeycomb feet," Sam repeated, delighted. "That's so cool."

Down below, something much slower was also climbing the wet wall: a snail, leaving a shiny trail behind it.

"Snails and slugs don't have sticky feet or hairs at all," said Tokay. "They glide along on **slime**, and their squishy foot ripples along, little wave after little wave."

Sam watched the snail inch upward, slow and steady.

"He's not fast," Sam said, "but he's not falling either."

"Slow and sticky wins the climb," said Tokay.

Sam tried wiggling across the ground like the snail, rippling his tummy along the floor. He only made it about one foot before collapsing into giggles.

"Needs more slime," said Tokay solemnly, and Sam laughed so hard he nearly rolled off the leaf.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Upside-Down Bats
chapters.text:
The leaf ride ended at the mouth of a dark little cave.

Sam peeked inside. Up on the ceiling, rows of bats hung upside down, fast asleep.

"Are THEY stuck with hairs too?" Sam whispered.

"Nope," said Tokay. "Bats can't zoom up walls fast like me. But they use curved little **claws** on their feet to hook onto the ceiling and just... hang there."

One bat shifted in its sleep, still hanging, perfectly safe.

"Like a coat hook," said Sam.

"Like a very furry coat hook," Tokay agreed.

Outside the cave, a sharp knocking sound rang out — *RAT-TAT-TAT-TAT!*

Sam jumped. "What's THAT?!"

A woodpecker was hammering its beak against a tree, climbing straight up the trunk without falling.

"Watch its feet," said Tokay.

Sam looked closer. The woodpecker had two toes pointing forward and two pointing backward, gripping the bark like four tiny anchors. Its stiff tail feathers pressed against the trunk like a little prop, holding it steady.

"He's basically sitting in a chair," Sam said.

"A chair made of his own tail," said Tokay. "Pretty clever bird."

The woodpecker gave one last *RAT-TAT-TAT* and flew off.

"That," said Sam, "was AWESOME."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Shelf
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Tokay. "My favorite one."

They landed on something smooth, enormous, and shiny — a real glass wall, the biggest Sam had ever seen.

A person was climbing straight up it, using two flat paddles pressed against the glass.

"That's a PERSON!" Sam shouted. "On a WALL! Like a gecko!"

"In the year **2014**," said Tokay proudly, "scientists built paddles shaped just like gecko feet. They let a real person climb a glass wall, just like me."

"People copied YOU," said Sam.

"People copied me," Tokay agreed, puffing up just a little.

Sam grinned. "That's the best thing I've ever heard."

Tokay's eyes glowed green again. The world spun, up and up and bigger and bigger.

**WHOOOOSH!**

Sam landed with a soft *bonk* back on his bedroom carpet, full-sized again. Tokay sat still on the shelf, glowing green, exactly where he always glowed.

Webster the spider dozed quietly in her jar.

Sam tiptoed over and peeked in. "You've got hairy feet too," he whispered. "I know your secret now."

He carried Webster's jar to the window and gently let her climb out onto the sill, back toward the garden, where spiders belong.

"Night, Tokay," Sam yawned, climbing into bed.

"Climb high, stick tight," Tokay whispered back, and glowed a little softer, just for Sam.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb high, stick tight.

true_facts.text: A gecko's toes have **millions of tiny hairs**, too small to see, which help it run up glass and walk upside down on ceilings.
Those tiny hairs split into even tinier tips that get so close to the wall they just hold on, like a soft **hug** — no glue needed.
A gecko's grip isn't glue, so its feet never get sticky or messy, and it can **peel** its toes off one at a time, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles have tiny pads that drip **sticky goo**, like little drops of glue, to help them climb.
Spiders have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet too, which is how so many spiders can climb straight up glass.
Ants and cockroaches use **sharp little claws** for bumpy walls, and switch to sticky pads for smooth ones.
Mountain goats climb steep rocky cliffs using hooves with a **hard edge and a soft, squishy middle** that molds around the rock.
Squirrels climb using **sharp, curved claws** that dig into tiny cracks and bumps too small for us to see.
Tree frogs have flat, sticky toe pads shaped like tiny **honeycombs**, which help them grip wet leaves and even wet glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding along on **slime**, rippling their squishy foot wave after wave.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff **tail feathers** as a prop, with two toes pointing forward and two pointing back.
In **2014**, scientists built sticky paddles shaped like gecko feet that let a real person climb up a glass wall.

new_recurring.rule: A plastic gecko night light on Sam's shelf that glows green every night. When an adventure begins, he blinks three times, his eyes flash bright green, and he peels a foot off the wall to speak. He always says the catchphrase 'Climb high…

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Sam returns to his bedroom full-sized, gently releases his garden spider Webster out the window toward the garden, and falls asleep as Tokay the night light glows softly on the shelf.

story.title: Finn, Nell, and the Honey Bee Adventure
story.subtitle: A tiny golden bee shows two sleepy kids how honey gets made.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Bee
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last sticky drop of honey off his toast. "Mmm," he said. "Honey is the best."

Nell held up her drawing. It showed one big yellow flower. "Yellow is the best," she said.

The bedroom was dark. Only one little light glowed.

It came from the windowsill. A tiny wooden bee sat there. Its wings began to hum. BZZZZZZ.

The little bee glowed gold, like a tiny sun. Finn sat straight up. Nell sat up too.

"Hello," said the bee. "My name is Buzz."

Finn's mouth fell wide open. "A talking bee!"

"I heard someone say the word honey," said Buzz. "Want to see how bees really make it?"

Nell hugged her flower drawing tight. "Can we see real flowers too?"

"Hold my wings," said Buzz, "and we will fly there together."

Finn grabbed one wing. Nell grabbed the other.

WHOOSH! The whole room spun gold and yellow.

Finn's tummy did a little flip. "Are we going to fall?" he asked.

"Bees never let go," said Buzz. "Hold tight, and you will not fall."

Finn held tight. The spinning slowed, then stopped.

When he opened his eyes, he was very, very small. So was Nell.

They stood on a big green leaf. Real flowers towered above them like giant yellow umbrellas.

"Welcome," said Buzz, "to the flower field."

Finn looked up, and up, and up. "Everything is SO big!"

"Or," said Buzz, smiling, "you are just bee-sized now."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Yellow Dust
chapters.text:
A big bee zoomed past. BZZZZZZ!

She landed on a giant yellow flower. Buzz said her name was Daisy.

Daisy poked a long, curly straw deep into the flower. Slurp, slurp, slurp.

"What is that?" asked Finn.

"That is her tongue," said Buzz. "It is called a proboscis. It is really just a long straw for drinking sweet flower juice. We call that juice nectar."

Finn tried saying it. "Pro-bos-cis." He giggled. "Funny word for a straw."

Nell pointed at Daisy's legs. "Why is she yellow there?"

Little yellow dust covered Daisy's legs like powder.

"That is pollen," said Buzz. "Flower dust. When bees fly to the next flower, some dust falls off. That helps flowers make new seeds and fruit."

Nell clapped both hands. "Pollen is yellow! My favorite color has a job!"

"Good noticing, Nell," said Buzz.

Finn spotted a flower with no bee on it at all. "Daisy, try this one!"

Daisy buzzed right over and landed where Finn had pointed.

Slurp, slurp, slurp.

"Good choice, Finn," said Buzz. "That flower is extra sweet today."

Finn puffed up proudly. He had picked the best flower in the whole field.

"Teamwork," said Nell, patting his shoulder like a grown-up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Honey Tummy
chapters.text:
Daisy's tummy looked round and fat now.

"Did she eat too much?" asked Finn.

Buzz laughed, a tiny buzzy laugh. "No. Bees have two tummies. One tummy is for food. The other tummy is only for carrying nectar home. We call it a honey stomach."

Nell gasped. "Two tummies! I only have one!"

"Why two?" asked Finn.

"That way," said Buzz, "the sweet juice stays clean. It does not mix up with her lunch."

Finn nodded slowly. "Smart bee."

Daisy buzzed up, up, up into the sky, her honey stomach full and round like a tiny balloon.

"Follow her!" shouted Finn.

Buzz zoomed after Daisy. Nell and Finn held tight, laughing as wind tickled their cheeks.

They flew over flowers. They flew over grass. Soon a big round shape rose ahead.

It smelled sweet. Almost like warm honey toast.

"There," said Buzz. "The hive."

Finn sniffed the air happily. "It smells like breakfast!"

Nell giggled so hard she almost fell off Buzz's wing. "Bee breakfast!"

"Hold on tight for landing," said Buzz. "Bump coming!"

They landed with a soft, bouncy THUMP on a tiny wooden step outside the hive.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: So Many Sisters
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, the buzzing was LOUD. BZZZZZZZZZZ!

Bees zoomed everywhere, busy as can be.

"How many bees live here?" asked Nell.

"In summer," said Buzz, "a hive can have twenty thousand bees. Sometimes even sixty thousand!"

Finn's eyes went huge. "That is more than all my toy cars put together!"

"And almost every single one," said Buzz, "is a girl. Sister bees do every job. They find flowers. They make honey. They keep the hive clean."

Nell threw her arms up. "GIRL POWER!"

In the middle of the hive sat one extra-big bee, moving slowly and calmly.

"That is the queen," said Buzz. "Her job is laying eggs. Sometimes more than a thousand eggs in one single day."

Finn tried to count on his fingers and gave up fast. "That is SO many eggs."

Nell tiptoed closer. "Hi, Queen Bee. Thank you for all your sisters."

The queen waggled gently, almost like she was saying thank you back.

Buzz smiled. "Nice manners, Nell. The queen likes you already."

Finn bowed low, the way he bowed to his grandma. The queen bee seemed to like that too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Honeycomb Rooms
chapters.text:
Finn looked at the walls. They were covered in tiny holes, lined up neat and tidy.

"What are these little rooms?" he asked.

"Honeycomb," said Buzz. "Each tiny room has six sides. We call that shape a hexagon."

Nell traced one with her finger. "One, two, three, four, five, six! You are right!"

"Where does the honeycomb come from?" asked Finn.

"Bees make it themselves," said Buzz. "Special spots on their tummies make soft wax, called beeswax. Bees chew it soft and build these little rooms."

Finn poked a wall gently. It felt a little soft, like warm candle wax. "Wow. Bee-made walls!"

Nell peeked into one tiny room. It was empty, waiting.

"What goes inside?" she asked.

"Watch," said Buzz, pointing to a bee flying in.

The bee tipped her head. A drop of nectar slid into the little room, shiny and gold.

Nell clapped. "A nectar cup!"

"Exactly," said Buzz. "Good eye, Nell."

Finn peeked into the next room over. It was already half full. "This hive is like a hundred tiny cupboards!"

"A hundred tiny, sticky cupboards," said Buzz, and Finn giggled so hard he nearly bumped his head.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Fanning Bees
chapters.text:
A whole row of bees lined up by the honeycomb. They flapped their wings so fast they blurred.

BZZZZZZZZZZZZ!

"Why are they fanning?" asked Nell, covering her ears just a little.

"Nectar is watery," said Buzz. "Fanning blows the water away. That turns it from runny juice into thick, sticky honey."

Finn flapped his arms like wings, trying to help. "Like this?"

"Almost," laughed Buzz. "Bee wings flap about two hundred times every second. That is what makes the buzzing sound you hear."

Nell flapped her arms super fast and giggled. "I can't go that fast!"

"Nobody can, except bees," said Buzz.

Finn leaned close to one little room. The nectar inside looked thicker than before, golden and shiny.

"It is turning into real honey!" he said.

Nell sniffed it. "It smells like toast already."

Finn noticed one little room that still looked watery and thin. "That one needs more fanning!" he said, pointing.

Two bees zoomed right over and flapped extra fast.

Buzz nodded. "Good spotting, Finn. Teamwork makes honey faster."

Finn grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "TEAMWORK MAKES HONEY!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Little Lid
chapters.text:
One bee stopped in front of a full honey room. She patted a thin wax lid over the top. PAT PAT PAT.

"Why cover it up?" asked Finn.

"That little lid keeps the honey safe and clean," said Buzz. "We call it a cap."

Nell peeked at a capped cell. "Like a tiny lunchbox lid!"

"Honey is special," said Buzz. "If it stays capped and dry, it never goes bad. Not ever. Honey found in very old places can still be good to eat."

Finn's eyes went huge. "Honey NEVER spoils? That is the best food in the whole world."

"Can I help put a lid on?" asked Nell.

"Gently now," said Buzz.

Nell pressed one tiny finger near a cell. The bee tapped the last bit of wax into place, right where Nell pointed.

"We did it together!" said Nell happily, bouncing on her toes.

Finn gave her a high five. "Teamwork again!"

Row after row of little lids sparkled gold down the whole wall, like tiny shining buttons.

"So much honey," whispered Finn. "No wonder it smells like breakfast in here."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Waggle Dance
chapters.text:
A bee near the entrance started wiggling in a funny pattern. Shake, shake, turn, shake!

Nell burst out laughing. "Is she dancing?"

"She is!" said Buzz. "We call it the waggle dance. It tells other bees which way to fly, and how far, to find good flowers."

Finn tried copying the wiggle, shaking side to side. "Like this?"

"Close enough for a human," giggled Buzz.

Nell joined in, wiggling straight toward the honeycomb and then pointing outside. "This way to the yellow flowers!"

The dancing bee buzzed off happily, flying exactly where Nell had pointed.

"She listened to Nell!" said Finn, amazed.

"It takes about twelve bees their whole lives," said Buzz, "just to make one teaspoon of honey."

Finn thought about his toast that morning. "That is a LOT of work for one yummy bite."

"That is why bees save it up," said Buzz. "All winter long, when flowers are gone, this honey is their food."

Nell nodded seriously, like a tiny teacher. "Smart bees. Saving snacks for later."

Finn patted the honeycomb wall softly. "Thank you for sharing your snacks with us too."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to Bed
chapters.text:
"Time to fly home," said Buzz gently.

Finn and Nell held his wings tight. WHOOSH! Gold light spun around them again, brighter and brighter.

When it stopped, Finn was back on his bedroom floor. Nell sat beside him, still holding her yellow flower drawing.

The little wooden bee sat quiet on the windowsill again, not glowing anymore.

On Finn's nightstand sat his small jar of honey, glowing just a tiny bit gold, like it remembered the whole adventure.

Nell looked down at her drawing. A tiny bee now sat on her yellow flower, where before there had been none at all.

"Did you draw that?" Finn asked.

Nell shook her head and smiled a secret smile.

Finn yawned a great big yawn. "Tomorrow, can we have honey toast again?"

"Tomorrow," whispered Buzz from the windowsill, so soft only a bee could hear it, "and maybe another adventure too."

Finn snuggled deep into his blanket. Nell hugged her flower drawing close to her chest.

Outside, somewhere far off, one last tiny BZZZZZZ floated by, like a goodnight kiss from the whole hive.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Buzz bright, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: A forager bee drinks sweet flower juice, called **nectar**, with a long straw-like tongue called a **proboscis**.
Yellow flower dust called **pollen** sticks to a bee's legs and helps flowers grow new seeds and fruit.
Bees have a second tummy just for nectar, called a **honey stomach**, so it stays separate from their food.
A hive can have **twenty thousand to sixty thousand bees** living together in summer.
The **queen bee** lays the eggs, sometimes **more than a thousand eggs in one day**.
Honeycomb is made of tiny rooms with **six sides**, called **hexagons**.
Bees make soft **beeswax** from special spots on their own tummies to build the honeycomb.
Bees **fan their wings** to blow away the water in nectar, turning it into thick, sticky honey.
A bee's wings flap about **two hundred times every second**, which makes the buzzing sound.
Bees seal each full honey room with a thin **wax lid**, called a cap, to keep it clean.
Honey kept sealed and dry **never spoils**, not even after a very long time.
A bee does a wiggly **waggle dance** to show other bees which way to fly to find good flowers.
It takes about **twelve bees their whole lives** to make just one teaspoon of honey.
Bees save up honey as food for **winter**, when there are no flowers to visit.

story.title: Omar and the Wheel That Remembered
story.subtitle: A BMX kid pedals through 200 years of bicycles.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Running Machine — 1817
chapters.text:
Omar lay on his bedroom floor, BMX bike flipped upside down, spinning the front wheel with one finger. He loved watching it blur into a silver circle. Everyone else in the house was asleep. Omar was supposed to be too.

He gave the wheel one more spin. This time it didn't slow down. It glowed sky blue and hummed, louder and louder, like a kazoo wearing a cape.

"Um," said Omar. "Wheels don't do that."

A tiny voice came from the hub, the little metal middle where all the spokes meet. "Most wheels don't talk, either. I'm Hub."

"You're a bike part," said Omar.

"I'm a bike *spirit*," said Hub. "Tonight you meet my great-great-great-grandwheels. Hop on."

The blue light swallowed the bedroom. When it let go, Omar stood in a muddy street that smelled like horses.

A man in a tall coat rolled past on a wooden two-wheeler, pushing the ground with his feet. No pedals anywhere.

"That's not a bike," Omar said. "He's not even pedaling — he's just running while sitting down!"

"Good eye," said Hub. "That's Karl von Drais. In **1817** he built the 'running machine' — a wooden bike with no pedals, steered by handlebars just like yours."

Omar hopped on the spare one leaning on a fence. He pushed off, feet scuffing the dirt. "This is basically a scooter wearing a bike costume!"

Von Drais laughed so hard he nearly fell off his own.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Boneshaker — 1860s
chapters.text:
CLANG. CLANG. CLANG. Something was rattling Omar's teeth before he even saw it.

They'd landed in Paris, decades later, where a man pedaled past on a wooden bike that bounced over every cobblestone.

"Whoa," Omar said, grabbing his own jaw. "That looks like it hurts."

"It did," said Hub. "French builders named Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement put pedals right on the front wheel in the **1860s**. People called it the 'boneshaker' because it shook your bones on bumpy streets."

"Two Pierres?" Omar grinned. "That's a lot of Pierre for one bike."

A kid about Omar's age offered him a turn. Omar pedaled, and the front wheel yanked the handlebars sideways. He wobbled, then figured out the trick: push gentle, steer gentler.

"You have to be smooth," Omar called back, "like landing a bunny hop!"

The other kids tried copying his smooth pedaling, and the rattling got a little less awful. Omar had just taught Paris its first bike lesson.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Penny-Farthing — 1870s
chapters.text:
The next wheel was enormous — taller than Omar, with a tiny wheel trailing behind like a little brother.

"That front wheel is the size of a trampoline," Omar said.

"It's called a penny-farthing," said Hub, "named after two old British coins — one huge, one tiny, like the wheels. Riders loved them in the **1870s** because one pedal turn went way farther."

"But how do you even get up there?"

A rider demonstrated — and stopped too fast. He tipped forward over the handlebars and landed in a hay pile with a soft WHUMP.

"That's called 'taking a header,'" Hub said. "It happened a lot. He's fine — just hay in his ears."

Omar studied the wheel, then pointed at the seat, way up high. "The problem isn't the wheel. It's that your seat's too close to the front. If you lean back more, you won't tip!"

The rider tried it, leaning back as he rode. He didn't fall once. "Smart kid!" he shouted.

Omar grinned. Fixing a 150-year-old bike problem before breakfast — not bad.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Safety Bicycle — 1885
chapters.text:
The next bike looked, for the first time, like an actual bike.

"Two wheels, same size!" Omar said. "Finally, something normal."

"This is John Kemp Starley's idea," said Hub. "In **1885** he built the Rover Safety Bicycle — even wheels, and a chain pulling the back wheel around. No more giant front wheel to fall off of."

Omar hopped on and pedaled a slow circle. It felt steady, solid, familiar — almost exactly like his own BMX bike.

"This is the ancestor of MY bike," Omar said, patting the frame. "Finally, someone invented the thing that makes sense."

Starley overheard and laughed. "Everyone kept falling off the tall ones. Seemed smart to build one you could actually land on your feet from."

"Trust me," Omar said, "landing on your feet is my whole specialty."

He did a little hop off the bike to prove it — and stuck the landing perfectly.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Bouncy Tire — 1888
chapters.text:
Omar's teeth were still buzzing from the last bumpy ride, so the next stop was a relief.

A man was wrapping a rubbery tube around a bike wheel and pumping it full of air.

"Why is the tire puffy?" Omar asked.

"This is John Boyd Dunlop," Hub said. "In **1888**, he invented the air-filled tire — a rubber tube pumped full of air, so the ride feels bouncy instead of bone-rattling. He made it for his son's tricycle."

Omar pushed down on the tire with his thumb. SPROING. It bounced right back.

"That's basically a trampoline for your wheel," Omar said.

Dunlop handed him a bike to test. Omar rode it over a bumpy patch and felt almost nothing. "Whoa! It's like riding on a cloud that knows how to steer!"

Dunlop beamed. "Told you it would catch on."

"Catch on?" said Omar. "People are gonna want this on EVERY wheel, even cars."

He wasn't wrong.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Golden Age — 1890s
chapters.text:
The street Omar landed on next was packed — bikes everywhere, bells ringing, a whole crowd of riders.

"Everyone has one!" Omar said.

"This is the **1890s**," said Hub, "the Golden Age of Bicycles. Millions got sold across Europe and America. And for women, it meant something huge — bikes let them travel on their own, whenever they wanted."

A woman rolled by wearing baggy riding pants called bloomers, instead of a long skirt that could get tangled in the wheel.

"Smart," Omar said. "Skirts and bike chains do NOT mix."

"A famous reformer named Susan B. Anthony said bicycles did more to help women get freedom than almost anything else," Hub added.

Omar watched a group of women race each other down the street, laughing, bells jingling. "That's not just a bike craze," Omar said. "That's everybody figuring out wheels equal freedom."

"Exactly," said Hub. "You get it."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Bike Shop in Dayton — 1890s
chapters.text:
A bell jingled over a shop door. Inside, two brothers were fixing a bike chain, tools everywhere.

"Wilbur and Orville Wright," Hub whispered. "They run a bike shop in Dayton, Ohio, in the **1890s** — before they invent anything that flies."

Omar's eyes went wide. "THE Wright brothers? The airplane guys? They fixed BIKES first?"

"They learned to build light metal frames and spoked wheels right here," Hub said. "Those same tricks helped them build their first flying machine."

Orville held up a thin metal tube. "Light but strong," he said. "Works for wheels. Why not wings?"

Omar grinned. "So basically — no bike shop, no airplane?"

"Basically," said Wilbur.

Omar looked down at his own bike tires. "My BMX bike is distant cousins with an airplane. That is extremely cool."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Back Home — Billions of Bikes
chapters.text:
The blue light swirled one more time, faster now, and Omar felt dirt turn to carpet under his feet.

Before the light faded all the way, Hub showed him one quick flash: dirt jumps, kids launching off ramps on small, tough bikes with knobby tires.

"That's BMX and mountain bikes," Hub said, "invented by riders in the **1970s** in America who wanted bikes tough enough for dirt and tricks."

"That's basically... my bike," Omar said, grinning.

"Today," Hub said, "there are more than a billion bikes on Earth. More than any other vehicle, anywhere."

Then Omar was home, flat on his bedroom carpet, his BMX bike right-side up beside him, front wheel slowly spinning to a stop.

Hub's glow faded to a tiny blue spark in the hub. "Same time tomorrow night?"

"Definitely," Omar whispered, pulling his blanket up. "Ride well, Hub."

The spark winked out, and the bedroom was quiet again.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ride well.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a German inventor named Karl von Drais built a wooden bike with no pedals — you pushed it along with your feet.
His invention could be steered with handlebars, just like bikes today.
In the **1860s**, two Frenchmen named Pierre put pedals right on the front wheel, making the bumpy 'boneshaker.'
In the **1870s**, the penny-farthing had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel.
Penny-farthings were named after two old coins, one big and one small.
Falling forward off a penny-farthing was called 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, John Kemp Starley built a safety bicycle with two same-size wheels and a chain, much like bikes today.
In **1888**, John Boyd Dunlop invented the air-filled tire, making rides bouncy instead of bone-rattling.
In the **1890s**, bicycles became super popular, with millions of bikes sold, called the Golden Age of Bicycles.
Bicycles let women travel on their own, and a reformer named Susan B. Anthony said bikes helped free them.
The Wright brothers, who later built the first airplane, used to run a bike repair shop in Dayton, Ohio.
They used bike-building skills, like light metal tubing and wheels, to help build their flying machine.
BMX and mountain bikes, tough and great for tricks, became popular in the United States in the **1970s**.
Today there are more than a billion bicycles in the world — more than any other kind of vehicle.

story.title: Ada and Bolt and the Secret of Magnets
story.subtitle: A glowing robot, a fridge magnet board, and the invisible pull that holds everything together.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Bolt Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Ada lay on her bedroom floor long after lights-out, snapping fridge magnet letters onto her little metal board. She loved watching the letters jump into place with a tiny CLICK.

Her favorite toy, a round robot named Bolt, sat on her shelf with his magnet-shaped head. Tonight his eyes blinked on, bright blue. "Hello, Ada," he said. "Ready to see how magnets really work?"

Ada sat up fast. "You can talk?"

"Only when something magnetic happens nearby," said Bolt. He hopped down, and the letter A leapt off the board and stuck to his chin. The letter B stayed put.

"Why did A stick but B didn't?" Ada asked.

Bolt said every magnet has two ends, called **poles** — north and south. "North and south pull together," he said. "But turn one around..."

Ada flipped Bolt's head. The letter A shot off and landed on her pillow.

"IT PUSHED AWAY!" Ada yelled.

"Same poles push apart. Opposite poles pull close," said Bolt. "That's the whole secret."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Invisible Hug
chapters.text:
Bolt's chest popped open like a tiny door. "Climb in," he said. "Time to see what we can't normally see."

Ada squeezed inside, and WHOOSH — they shrank down tiny, right next to a fridge magnet.

Swirly glowing lines curved from one end of the magnet to the other.

"That's the **magnetic field**," said Bolt. "The invisible space around a magnet where its pull and push work."

Ada reached out. The lines tickled her fingers, tugging them gently toward the magnet.

"People can even see its shape," Bolt said, "by sprinkling tiny iron bits nearby. The bits line up along the curvy lines, just like this."

Ada traced one curved line all the way around. "It's like the magnet is hugging the air!"

"Best hug in science," said Bolt.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Spinning Tiny Dancers
chapters.text:
Back at full size, Bolt pointed at Ada's toy box. "Quick test. Which of your things are magnetic?"

Ada touched a metal spoon, a plastic block, and a soda can to Bolt's chin.

The spoon stuck. CLICK! The plastic did nothing. The soda can did nothing too, even though it looked like metal.

"Huh?" said Ada.

Bolt explained that inside magnetic things, like iron, are tiny bits called **electrons** — too small to see, spinning like little tops. In magnetic metal, they line up facing the same way, like a marching band, and that makes the whole thing magnetic.

"In wood, plastic, and some metals like your can," Bolt said, "those tiny bits point every which way. No marching band, no magnet."

Ada tapped the can again. Still nothing. "Sorry, can. You're just not in the band."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Old Rock and the Old Compass
chapters.text:
Bolt's head whirred, and the room shimmered into a dusty hillside. "Long ago, in a place called Magnesia, people found rocks that pulled on iron all by themselves."

Ada picked up a pretend rock. It tugged gently at her toy spoon. "Whoa, it's already magnetic!"

"That rock is called **lodestone**," said Bolt. "Some think that's even where the word magnet comes from."

The hillside shimmered into an old boat deck. A traveler held a floating lodestone that kept turning to point one way.

"More than two thousand years ago, people in China used lodestones like this," said Bolt, "to make the first **compasses** — tools that always point the same direction."

Ada held the floating stone steady. "It's like it already knows which way to go!"

"Sort of," said Bolt, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Earth's Giant Magnet
chapters.text:
"Where does the compass point?" Ada asked.

"Follow me," said Bolt.

They zoomed up until Earth hung below them like a big blue marble. "Deep inside, melted iron swirls around and around," said Bolt. "That makes the whole planet act like one giant magnet."

Ada gasped. "The whole Earth is a magnet?"

"Yep. That's why a compass needle swings north," said Bolt. "It lines up with Earth's pull, just like your letters line up with mine."

Ada spun slowly, pretending to be a needle, until she faced the same way as Bolt's glowing arrow.

"Some animals use it too," Bolt added. "Birds and sea turtles may feel Earth's magnet to find their way on long trips."

"Lucky turtles," said Ada. "I need a map."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Switch It On!
chapters.text:
Back on her bedroom floor, Bolt pulled a loop of wire from his chest and wound it round a nail. "Watch this."

He pressed a tiny button. The wrapped nail buzzed and snapped a paperclip off the carpet.

"IT'S MAGNETIC NOW!" Ada shouted.

"That's an **electromagnet**," said Bolt. "A magnet made with wire and electricity, and you can switch it on and off."

He pressed the button again. The paperclip dropped. On, pull. Off, drop.

"Doorbells use these," Bolt said. "So do loudspeakers, and giant cranes at junkyards that lift whole old cars."

Ada pressed the button herself, giggling as the paperclip jumped and fell, jumped and fell. "Best light switch ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Snap the Magnet
chapters.text:
Ada looked at the little bar magnet on Bolt's shelf. "What happens if you break one in half?"

"Try it," said Bolt, handing her a snap-apart toy magnet.

SNAP! It broke into two pieces.

Ada touched a paperclip to the first piece. It stuck. She touched it to the second piece. It stuck too.

"Wait, both halves work?!" she said.

"Every piece gets its own north end and south end," said Bolt. "Break a magnet in half, and you don't get a lonely north and a lonely south. You get two whole new magnets."

Ada snapped the pieces apart again, testing each bit. Every single one still pulled the paperclip close.

"Magnets," she said, "really don't like being lonely."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back to the Fridge
chapters.text:
Bolt walked Ada back to her magnet board and stretched one of her floppy fridge magnets. It bent like rubber without falling apart.

"Your fridge magnets are soft like this," Bolt said, "because they're bendy rubber mixed with tiny bits of magnet powder. That's why they bend around corners and still stick tight."

Ada pressed the letter A back onto the board. CLICK. It held, just like always, only now she knew why.

She yawned a giant yawn. Bolt's blue eyes dimmed, settling back onto her shelf.

"Will you wake up again?" Ada whispered.

"Whenever something magnetic happens," said Bolt. "Which, in your room, is basically always."

Ada smiled and pulled up her blanket, the little letter A glowing faintly on her board.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Keep sticking together.

true_facts.text: A magnet has two ends called **poles**, a north one and a south one.
Opposite poles pull together, and the same poles push apart.
The **magnetic field** is the invisible space around a magnet where its push and pull work.
Sprinkling tiny iron bits near a magnet shows the curvy lines of its field.
Inside magnetic things like iron are tiny spinning bits called **electrons**.
In magnetic metal, those tiny bits line up facing the same way, like a marching band.
A naturally magnetic rock called **lodestone** was found long ago near a place called Magnesia.
More than two thousand years ago, people in China used lodestones to make the first **compasses**.
Deep inside Earth, swirling melted iron makes the whole planet act like a giant magnet.
A compass needle swings north because it lines up with Earth's magnetic pull.
An **electromagnet** is a magnet made with wire and electricity, and it can switch on and off.
Electromagnets are used in doorbells, loudspeakers, and giant junkyard cranes that lift old cars.
Break a magnet in half and you don't get a lonely north and south — you get two whole new magnets.
Fridge magnets are made of bendy rubber mixed with tiny bits of magnet powder, so they can bend without falling apart.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow That Wouldn't Hold Still
story.subtitle: A sunset, a water pistol, and a tiny sprite made of bent light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Spray That Sparkled
chapters.text:
Dev lay on his bedroom carpet, water pistol loaded, aiming at absolutely nothing. Priya sat beside him, drawing a rainbow that kept coming out lopsided.

"Mine looks like a squished worm," she said, crossing out purple for the third time.

The last gold strip of sunset slid through the blinds. Dev could not resist. He pulled the trigger. **SPLOOSH!** A fan of tiny drops floated through the sunbeam — and a stripe of colors flickered across the wall.

Both kids froze. The stripe wobbled, then peeled itself off the wall and hovered, a tiny glowing triangle no bigger than a coin.

"Hello," it said. "I'm Pip. You just made a rainbow — and I happen to live inside them."

"Inside a *rainbow*?" Dev dropped his water pistol.

"Sunlight dives into a water drop, bends, bounces off the back wall inside, and bends again on the way out," Pip said. "That bending is called **refraction** — light changes direction when it goes from air into water."

Priya grinned. "So my drawing was right. Rainbows ARE bendy."

"Want to see where the rest of the bends happen?" Pip asked. He spun once, and the bedroom wall dissolved into a hallway made of light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Secret Rainbow Hiding in White
chapters.text:
They stepped into a glowing room that looked like the inside of a flashlight.

"Quick riddle," said Pip. "What color is sunlight?"

"Yellow," said Dev.

"Trick question," said Priya, tapping her chin like a true artist. "I bet it's secretly every color at once."

"Got it in one," said Pip. "Sunlight only looks white, but it's really every color mixed together. A raindrop sorts them back out, because each color bends by a slightly different amount."

Colors spilled out of a glowing drop in front of them, lining up in order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, deep blue, and purple.

"People remember that order with a made-up name," Pip said. "**Roy G. Biv**."

Dev wrinkled his nose. "Weird name for a guy."

"I've got a better one," Priya said. "Rude Old Yaks Gobble Bananas In Vans."

Dev cackled so hard he nearly fell off the glowing floor.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Red on the Outside, Purple on the In
chapters.text:
"Why's red always on the outside?" Priya asked, pointing at the lineup of colors.

"Because red bends the least, and purple bends the most," said Pip. "**Red** ends up on the outer edge, and **violet** tucks in on the inside, every single time."

Dev tugged Pip's glowing edge. "Can WE make a rainbow? Like, on purpose?"

"Two things," said Pip. "The sun has to be behind you, and rain — or spray — has to be in front."

Dev spun around until the sunbeam-hallway's glow sat right behind his shoulders, then raised his water pistol and fired. **WHOOSH!** A little arc of color curved in front of him.

"IT WORKED BECAUSE I TURNED AROUND!" Dev shouted.

"Exactly," said Pip. "You just aimed yourself, not just the water."

Priya clapped. "Best trick shot ever, Dev."
chapters.shout_line: IT WORKED BECAUSE I TURNED AROUND!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Whole Round Circle
chapters.text:
"Rain plus sunshine," Pip said, floating ahead. "That's the real secret. Most rainbows show up during or right after a shower, the second the sun peeks back out."

"So that's why they're after rain," Priya said, writing it on an invisible glowing notepad Pip had handed her.

"Here's a weirder bit," said Pip. "Rainbows are actually full circles. We only see the top half because the ground is in the way."

Dev gasped. "Then where's the BOTTOM half hiding?"

"Right under your feet, blocked by the dirt," said Pip.

Priya grabbed her glowing pencil and drew a complete ring instead of an arc. "Like that?"

"Exactly like that," said Pip, and the drawing floated up and hung in the air, a perfect circle of color.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Kids, Two Different Rainbows
chapters.text:
"People in airplanes sometimes see the whole circle," Pip went on, "because there's no ground up there to chop it in half."

Dev pressed his face against an imaginary airplane window. "I want to see a whole one."

"Someday," said Pip. "For now, try this." He had Priya stand on one spot and Dev stand three steps away, both facing the same glowing drop-cloud.

"Fire when ready," said Pip.

They sprayed together. Two arcs of color shimmered — but not in quite the same place.

"Hey! Mine's higher than yours!" Dev said.

"That's because every single person sees their own personal rainbow," said Pip. "It depends on exactly where your eyes are standing."

Priya laughed. "So nobody's ever stolen my rainbow. It was only ever mine."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Upside-Down Extra One
chapters.text:
As the two arcs glowed, a second, fainter stripe of color appeared above the first one.

Dev squinted. "Why's the top one backwards?"

"Good eye," said Pip. "Sometimes light bounces twice inside a raindrop instead of once. That makes a second rainbow — fainter, and with its colors flipped."

"So it's an echo rainbow," said Priya.

"I like that," said Pip. "Keep it."

Dev tried to touch the top one and his finger went right through the glow. "Hah! I'm basically magic."

"DOUBLE RAINBOW!" Dev shouted, and Priya shouted it right back, just to tease him.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Mist, Waterfalls, and a Trick You Can't Win
chapters.text:
Pip led them past a glowing waterfall, a cloud of hose mist, and a crescent moon. "Rainbows show up anywhere light meets tiny drops," he said. "Waterfalls, garden hoses, even moonlight — though a moon-made one is so faint it mostly looks gray."

"Boo. I want a sparkly one," said Dev.

"Some old stories say there's a pot of gold waiting at the end of a rainbow," Pip said. "That part's probably just a fun old tale, not something true, because a rainbow's end moves the second you move."

Dev took off running toward the glowing arc anyway, water pistol bouncing on his hip.

"You can't catch it, Dev!" Priya called, giggling.

Sure enough, the arc stayed exactly the same distance away, no matter how fast Dev's sneakers slapped the floor. He skidded to a stop, panting. "Rude old yaks gobble bananas, and apparently rainbows RUN."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Man With the Glass Triangle
chapters.text:
Pip slowed near a cozy, candlelit room with a man bent over a dusty table.

"That's **Isaac Newton**," Pip whispered. "Back in the **1660s**, he shone sunlight through a glass triangle called a **prism** and watched it split into the very same colors as a rainbow. It proved sunlight had every color hiding inside it all along."

"Like our glowing drop did," Priya said.

"Exactly like that," said Pip. "People have been curious about rainbows forever. One old story even calls a rainbow a bridge — **Bifrost** — connecting earth to the home of the gods."

Dev yawned a yawn the size of a whole rainbow. "I want to go home now."

Pip smiled and spun them gently back through the glowing hallway, which folded itself down into one small sunbeam, then into the last light sneaking through the blinds.

They landed back on the carpet. Priya's drawing now had a perfect round rainbow on it, red on the outside, violet tucked inside. Pip shrank down to a tiny speck of light and tucked himself into the corner of her paper, where he'd be waiting next time a sunbeam came by.

"Goodnight, Pip," Priya whispered.

Dev was already asleep, one hand still curled around his water pistol.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Keep catching the light.

true_facts.text: A rainbow happens when sunlight dives into a raindrop, bends, bounces off the back inside, and bends again on its way out.
That bending is called **refraction**, and it happens because light changes direction going from air into water.
Sunlight looks white, but it's secretly made of every color mixed together.
People remember the rainbow's color order with the name **Roy G. Biv**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet.
**Red** sits on the outside of a rainbow and **violet** on the inside, because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun has to be behind you and the rain, or spray, has to be in front.
Rainbows are actually whole circles — we usually just see the top half because the ground blocks the rest.
From an airplane, with no ground in the way, people sometimes spot a full circle rainbow.
Every person actually sees their own personal rainbow, made from their own raindrops at their own angle.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow shows up above the first one, with its colors flipped around.
Rainbows can also appear in waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, called a **moonbow**.
Long ago, in the **1660s**, **Isaac Newton** used a glass **prism** to split sunlight into the same rainbow colors.
You can never actually walk up and touch a rainbow, because it moves the moment you move.

story.title: Jack and Ellie and the Mermaid's Purse
story.subtitle: A swim through four hundred million years of sharks

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Mermaid's Purse
chapters.text:
It was bath time. Then it was way past bath time. Jack sat on his bedroom floor, sorting shells from the beach.

Ellie knelt next to him in her mermaid-tail blanket. She held up a flat, leathery pouch with curly tips. "This one's magic," she said. "It's a mermaid's purse."

Jack grinned his big-brother grin. "That's not a mermaid's purse, Ellie. That's a—"

Before he could finish, the pouch began to glow soft green. It hummed, low and steady, like a sleepy bee.

Then it went POP, and water poured out. Not onto the carpet — up and around them, swirling like moonlight.

"JACK!" Ellie grabbed his arm.

"HOLD ON!" he shouted, snatching a dive flipper from his bag.

Down, down, down they spun, and landed with a soft SPLOOSH in a warm, blue sea.

A grey shape glided past, its tail swishing side to side.

"Is that a shark?" Ellie whispered, pressing close.

"I think so," said Jack. "But everything feels so old."

A warm voice answered from the water. "Good eye. You've landed **more than 400 million years ago** — before dinosaurs, before even trees."

A woman in an old diving mask swam up, smiling. "I'm Eugenie. Folks call me the Shark Lady. I study sharks. I always have."

Jack watched the shark bend smoothly around a rock. "Its body curves so easily," he said. "Like it doesn't have real bones."

"Sharp eyes," said Eugenie. "A shark's skeleton isn't hard bone like yours. It's made of **cartilage** — bendy stuff, like the stretchy part at the top of your ear. Feel it."

Both kids squeezed their own ears. "Whoa," said Ellie. "Bendy ear-bones."

"Exactly," Eugenie laughed. "That's how sharks twist and turn so well."

Ellie put her hands on her hips. "I still say it's magic. Even if a shark made the purse."

Jack laughed. "Fair enough. Mermaid's purse it is."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Tooth the Size of a Hand
chapters.text:
A current tugged them sideways, through blue water gone grey and murky.

They landed on a seabed scattered with huge, triangle-shaped shapes, half-buried in sand.

"Teeth," Jack breathed. "Giant teeth."

He dug one free. It was heavier than his whole hand, with jagged edges like a steak knife.

"That belonged to **megalodon**," said Eugenie. "A giant shark that's not around anymore. People only know about it from teeth like that one."

Ellie's eyes went wide. "Not around anymore? Where did it go?"

"It lived a very, very long time ago," said Eugenie gently, "and then it stopped existing, like the dinosaurs did. We call that **extinct**."

Jack held the tooth up against his own hand to check the size. They matched, edge to edge.

"A shark's soft, bendy bones don't usually last underground," Eugenie explained. "But hard teeth do. So almost everything we know about megalodon comes from teeth just like this."

"So this tooth is basically a clue," Jack said.

"Exactly right," said Eugenie, ruffling his hair.

Ellie picked up a smaller tooth and tucked it behind her ear like a treasure. "Good thing the tooth fairy isn't down here," she said. "She'd need a much bigger pillow."

Jack snorted so hard a bubble shot out of his nose, and even Eugenie laughed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
The water brightened. A shadow the size of a school bus drifted overhead.

Ellie froze. Then she saw its mouth — wide open, but calm, almost sleepy.

"Don't worry," said Eugenie. "That's a **whale shark**. It's the biggest fish in the whole ocean, over **40 feet long** — but it only eats tiny floating bits of food, smaller than rice."

"That's HUGE for something that eats tiny snacks," Jack said.

Ellie swam a little closer, careful not to touch, and started counting the pale spots across its back. "One, two, three, four..."

"Keep going," said Eugenie. "No two whale sharks have the same spot pattern. Like a fingerprint."

"Fourteen!" Ellie called out, giving up around its tail.

"Some whale sharks live **100 years or more**," said Eugenie. "Longer than almost any other fish."

"A hundred birthdays," Ellie said softly. "That's a lot of birthday cake."

The whale shark swished its tail and glided on, unbothered, like a gentle grey cloud.

Jack waved. "Bye, big guy."

"SPLOOSH," said Ellie happily, waving too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Rows and Rows of Teeth
chapters.text:
A sleek, pale shape cut through the water ahead — faster, sharper, all business.

"Great white," Jack whispered, half thrilled, half nervous.

Eugenie tapped a floating glass bubble, and it opened like a little submarine. "Hop in. We'll watch from somewhere safe."

Inside, Jack pressed close to the glass. The shark swam near, and its mouth opened just enough to show off rows and rows of pointed teeth, each edge like a tiny saw.

"A great white can grow up to **20 feet long**," said Eugenie, "with teeth built for catching fish and seals."

"Why so many rows?" Jack asked.

"Sharks lose teeth their whole lives," said Eugenie. "New ones keep moving forward to replace them, like a conveyor belt."

"A never-ending tooth machine," Jack said, grinning.

Ellie reached out and touched the glass where the shark's side brushed past. "Its skin looks bumpy."

"Good catch," said Eugenie. "Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny tooth-shaped bumps. It feels rough, like sandpaper, and it helps sharks slide smoothly through the water."

"Sandpaper fish," Ellie said. "Mermaids would never wear that as a dress."

"Good thing you're not a mermaid, then," Jack teased, and she splashed him right through the glass's little air vent.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Wide, Wobbly Head
chapters.text:
Something strange floated into view — a shark with a head shaped like a hammer.

Ellie burst out laughing. "Why does its head look like THAT?"

"That's a **hammerhead shark**," said Eugenie. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart, almost all the way around. That gives it a wraparound view of the whole ocean."

"Like eyes in the back of your head," Jack said. "Mom has those."

Ellie giggled. "She really does."

"There's more," said Eugenie. "Along its snout are tiny jelly-filled dots. They feel the faint electric buzz that every animal gives off, even one hiding under the sand."

Jack's mouth dropped open. "It can feel electricity?"

"Tiny amounts," Eugenie nodded. "Enough to find a hidden fish for dinner."

The hammerhead swung its wide head slowly side to side, scanning the sand below, and then zeroed in on something buried and dug it up in one quick motion.

"Found it," Jack said, pointing. "Right where it was looking."

"Nothing gets past that head," said Eugenie, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Shark That Walks
chapters.text:
The current carried them up into shallow, sunlit water, dotted with coral and little pools.

Something small and spotted flip-flopped across the sand on paddle-shaped fins.

"Is that shark... WALKING?" Ellie gasped.

"The **epaulette shark** can do exactly that," said Eugenie. "It walks across coral reefs and tide pools using its fins like little legs. It can even go hours without much oxygen, the stuff we breathe from the air."

Jack's competitive spark lit up. "Race you across the pool!"

He scrambled along the sand on hands and knees while the little shark flip-flopped beside him, surprisingly fast.

The shark won by a fin-tip.

Jack flopped back, laughing. "Beaten by a shark with LEGS."

"Technically fins," Ellie pointed out, grinning.

"Technically still embarrassing," Jack said, and even Eugenie couldn't hold back a laugh.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady's Lesson
chapters.text:
They drifted into calmer, open water, where Eugenie slowed and turned to face them.

"I spent my whole life studying sharks," she said. "Watching them, swimming with them, even training some to do little tasks."

"Training a SHARK?" Jack asked. "Like a dog?"

"Sort of," Eugenie smiled. "It showed people sharks are curious. They can learn."

Ellie hugged her own arms. "Are they scary, though? Everyone says sharks are scary."

"Shark attacks on people are very rare," said Eugenie gently. "Much rarer than people think. In fact, people harm far more sharks than sharks ever harm us."

Jack frowned. "That doesn't seem fair. Sharks keep the ocean balanced, right?"

"They do," said Eugenie. "Sharks sit at the top of the ocean's food chain. They help keep everything else healthy, from the biggest fish to the smallest."

"So... we should be on their side," Ellie said slowly.

"Lots of people are, now," said Eugenie, smiling warmly. "More every year."

Jack looked back at all the sharks they'd met — gentle, fast, strange, enormous, tiny. "They're not scary," he said. "They're just... sharks being sharks."

"Well said," Eugenie replied.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Through the Purse
chapters.text:
The water began to swirl again, gently this time, pulling them up and up.

"Wait!" Ellie called to Eugenie. "Will we see you again?"

Eugenie smiled, already fading into the blue. "Whenever the purse glows, I'll be close by."

Then came the SPLOOSH, and Jack and Ellie tumbled back onto the bedroom carpet, dry as toast, shells scattered around them.

The leathery pouch sat quiet now, dark and still, its glow all used up.

Ellie turned it over in her hands. "So it really is a mermaid's purse," she said. "Just... a shark made it. Some sharks lay their eggs inside pouches exactly like this one."

"Mermaid's purse," Jack agreed, "shark edition."

On the carpet beside it lay a small, smooth tooth, the one Ellie had tucked behind her ear. It hadn't come home empty-handed after all.

Jack yawned a yawn the size of a whale shark's mouth. Ellie yawned right back, matching him exactly.

They climbed into their beds, the little tooth tucked safely on the nightstand between them.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well, and dream of the deep blue sea.

true_facts.text: Sharks appeared in the ocean **more than 400 million years ago** — before dinosaurs or trees.
A shark's skeleton is made of **cartilage**, bendy stuff like the top of your ear, not hard bone.
**Megalodon** was a giant shark that isn't around anymore — scientists mostly know about it from its teeth.
Because soft shark bones don't usually last underground, almost everything we know about megalodon comes from **fossil teeth**.
The **whale shark** is the biggest fish in the ocean, over **40 feet long**, but it eats mostly tiny bits of food.
Some whale sharks live **100 years or more**.
A great white shark can grow up to **20 feet long** and has rows of sharp, saw-edged teeth.
Shark skin is covered in thousands of tiny bumps, making it feel like **sandpaper** and helping it swim smoothly.
A **hammerhead shark's** wide head spreads its eyes apart for a wraparound view of the ocean.
Tiny jelly-filled dots on a shark's snout can feel the faint electric buzz of hidden animals.
The **epaulette shark** can walk across reefs and tide pools using its fins like little legs.
Scientist Eugenie Clark, the **Shark Lady**, studied sharks for her whole life and showed they are curious and can learn.
Shark attacks on people are **very rare** — people harm far more sharks than sharks harm people.
Some sharks lay their eggs in leathery pouches nicknamed **'mermaid's purses.'**
